The girl reported that her mother rubbed a seeded spice on her face, mouth and throat, which burned and made her vomit, and threatened her with a knife. Investigators say the mother also forced the girl into the shower, hit her there and cut her hair with scissors. Officers documented large bruises consistent with belt strikes and arrested her Tuesday; KSL is withholding her name to protect the victim's identity.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: McDonald's expects inflation to keep traffic flat, shares dip after $8.5 billion capex plan
item.description: McDonald's told investors Wednesday that industrywide customer traffic in its key markets will likely stay flat while inflation remains high, sending its shares down as much as 6.5% to a near four-year low of $234.03. The chain simultaneously announced an $8.5 billion, decade-long support package for franchisees bearing costs under its "NEXT" strategy, plus targets for restaurant productivity and operating margins in the low- to mid-50% range by 2030. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the winners will be companies that create more demand and deliver it more efficiently. New U.S. business head Skye Anderson acknowledged the company had fallen short on consistent execution and must improve restaurant operations. The warning follows a second quarter in which McDonald's missed U.S. sales growth estimates and blamed missteps in winning back lower-income diners; its stock is down about 22% this year.
item.dc:creator: Anuja Bharat Mistry and Waylon Cunningham, Reuters

item.title: FBI investigating hackers' claim of stolen sensitive employee data, compromised jobs website
item.description: The FBI said Wednesday it is investigating claims by the hacking group ShinyHunters that it stole sensitive data on thousands of agents and job applicants and compromised the FBIJobs.gov portal. The bureau said the point of breach remains undetermined and that it is working with third-party providers supporting the site to limit risk; the portal was still offline Wednesday afternoon. A message circulating online and addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel and cyber division chief Brett Leatherman claimed the group holds data on nearly all FBI agents and applicants. The claims could not be independently verified, and an email to an address linked to the group went unanswered. ShinyHunters also demanded the bureau retract or correct a May public advisory describing it as a criminal group specializing in large-scale breaches and extortion.
item.dc:creator: Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: Disney to raise prices on Disney+, Hulu subscriptions, Bloomberg News reports
item.description: Disney will raise prices across several streaming plans, Bloomberg News reported Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The ad-free Disney+ tier is set to climb $2.50, or 13%, to $21.49 a month, and ad-free Hulu rises by the same amount, while the ad-free Disney+ and Hulu bundle goes up $2 to $21.99. Standalone ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu plans each increase 50 cents to $12.49, though the ad-supported bundle stays at $12.99. Customers were expected to be notified of the changes as early as Wednesday, and Disney did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The move follows a broader industry pattern of raising prices and leaning on ad-supported tiers, and comes a week after Disney named Karandeep Anand its first chief technology officer and promoted Adam Smith to lead streaming.
item.dc:creator: Anzar Mehraj, Reuters

item.title: Idaho high school is victim of alleged 'swatting' hoax, deputies say
item.description: The Bonneville County Sheriff's Office says Bonneville High School near Idaho Falls was targeted by a swatting hoax Wednesday after a reported threat near the campus around 11 a.m. Swatting involves false emergency reports designed to draw a heavy law enforcement response, creating chaos and risk of injury, according to the FBI. Bonneville School District 93 alerted parents that the school had entered a hall check over a possible weapon on campus and asked people to stay away while officers investigated. A hall check keeps students and staff inside classrooms while instruction continues, one of four emergency procedures alongside evacuation, reverse evacuation and lockdown. Deputies checked the area as a precaution, found no violence or actual threat, and lifted the hall check after roughly 45 minutes.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlyn Hart, EastIdahoNews.com

item.title: 'How else am I supposed to discipline them?' man accused of choking child asks police
item.description: Jason James Quigley, 36, of Santaquin, was charged Wednesday in 4th District Court with four counts of aggravated child abuse, a first-degree felony, plus obstruction of justice and public intoxication. Police were called Sunday after a 9-year-old ran to a neighbor's home reporting that Quigley was choking a 5-year-old at the residence. When officers questioned him, Quigley asked what else he was supposed to do to discipline the children and admitted drinking heavily, according to a booking affidavit; the younger child was found hiding under a bed. Both children told investigators Quigley believed they had stolen a cellphone. Prosecutors also allege he drove them up Goshen Canyon and held each over the river while threatening to drop them, saying he was testing them.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: McDonald's to create tiered loyalty program to lure repeat visitors
item.description: McDonald's will restructure its loyalty program into tiers, chief marketing officer Morgan Flatley said at the chain's investor day Wednesday, aiming to distinguish frequent customers from occasional ones. Flatley did not give a launch date or the number of tiers, but described three groups: about 220 million members worldwide who visit monthly or at least every 90 days, and roughly 150 million who have not eaten there in months. Frequent visitors could get faster points, early access to limited-time menu items and invitations to launch events, while mid-tier members may see game-like online challenges; lapsed members would be targeted with perks such as a birthday bonus. U.S. members can expect Uber ride credits and Disney+ subscriptions this year. CEO Chris Kempczinski said loyalty members account for about 30% of sales, and the shift follows a broader restaurant-industry move away from broad discounting that Starbucks made in January.
item.dc:creator: Waylon Cunningham, Reuters

item.title: Utah group to hold vigil honoring state's 2026 murder victims
item.description: Utah Homicide Survivors will hold a candlelight vigil at the State Capitol on Friday at 7 p.m. to mark the National Day of Remembrance for Homicide Victims. The service is set to include a memory garden, speeches and live music honoring Utahns killed and supporting their families. Among the scheduled speakers is a sister of Summer Roney, who was found slain in the back seat of her ex-boyfriend's car nearly two years ago. State officials and the FBI generally publish annual murder figures at year's end. Prominent 2026 cases include three people killed in Wayne County in March and two found dead in a Kearns home in April in what was later described as a domestic dispute.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Construction on SR 224 in Park City nears end, UDOT says
item.description: The Utah Department of Transportation and High Valley Transit say two major projects along state Route 224 in Park City are wrapping up after months of work. Crews are finishing new turning lanes at Deer Valley Drive and Park Avenue, with additional work concluding near Kimball Junction. High Valley Transit said one more paving job is scheduled for next week and that most construction should be done by the end of October. The work supports a larger bus rapid transit project linking Kimball Junction and Old Town. Bus service on that line is expected to begin in 2028.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Spanish Fork City Council approves changes to city code for data centers
item.description: The Spanish Fork City Council voted to amend city code, clearing a path for a proposed data center to move forward. Mayor Mike Mendenhall said the council weighed residents' concerns, particularly over water use, noting the city meters its water and could halt supply if needed. Jeff Chavez, CEO of Volition, the company behind the project, said its closed-loop cooling system uses roughly as much water as one or two Utah households. Council members also capped the city at a single data center unless a future vote changes that limit.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Utah hits new record for price of diesel fuel
item.description: Diesel in Utah reached a record $6.58 per gallon on Wednesday, according to AAA — two cents above Tuesday, 44 cents above a week earlier and $2.85 higher than a year ago. GasBuddy's head of petroleum analysis, Patrick De Haan, told KSL the increase traces largely to geopolitics, citing Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and disruption at the Strait of Hormuz tied to the U.S. and Israeli conflict with Iran. He said the refinery attacks became more damaging once the strait was closed, leaving Middle East refining capacity bottled up. GasBuddy pegged Salt Lake City diesel at $6.61, with regular unleaded just under $5. De Haan said the U.S. faces a tight diesel market rather than an outright shortage, and cautioned that a diesel export ban under consideration by the Trump administration would bring complications.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Zelenskyy, at UN, urges leaders to keep choking Russia's revenues and impede its war efforts
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday that Russia's revenues must remain a target, arguing that trade with Moscow buys the war more time. Speaking in English, he cast doubt on Putin's willingness to end the fighting, calling him "Patient Zero" from whom war keeps spreading. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the Security Council the same day that Moscow is willing to negotiate a lasting peace but will not accept a mere pause, which he said would let Ukraine and its backers rearm. Russia is scheduled to address the assembly Saturday, with Lavrov again standing in for Putin, who has not attended in years. Western analysts estimate more than 500,000 Russian troops killed and over 500,000 Ukrainian military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths, in a war now past four and a half years with front lines largely static.
item.dc:creator: Edith M. Lederer and Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press

item.title: World's largest copper mine halts operations after worker death
item.description: BHP suspended all operations Wednesday at Escondida in Chile, the world's largest copper mine, after a worker was killed in an accident during maintenance work. The union representing the site told Reuters the accident involved a front-end loader of a type commonly used in the industry. BHP gave no timeline for restarting; under Chilean practice, mines typically resume after a fatality only once inspectors confirm conditions are safe. Escondida sits in the Atacama Desert and is operated by BHP, with Rio Tinto holding a 30% stake and Japan's JECO Corp 12.5%. The company had projected output of up to 1.28 million metric tons of copper at the site this year.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Food insecurity up by 100K, Utah Food Bank reports. Here's a way to help
item.description: The Utah Food Bank reports that nearly 100,000 more Utahns are facing food insecurity than a year ago, bringing the state's total closer to 600,000 people. Demand typically climbs in fall and winter as household expenses rise and children spend more time out of school. America First Credit Union is collecting nonperishable food and cash donations at its branches, and director of public relations Dave Nellis said the contributions are distributed to six food pantries and organizations statewide. Donors do not need to be credit union members to participate. Nellis said small contributions add up, describing the goal as feeding neighbors and strengthening the community.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Fired IT employee accused of hacking Utah city emails, posting on Facebook
item.description: Wesley Fullenwider, 31, of Vineyard, was charged Wednesday in 4th District Court with unlawful computer access gaining confidential information, a third-degree felony, plus two misdemeanor counts of unlawful computer access. Prosecutors say the former contract IT technician kept getting into Vineyard city email accounts after the city asked in January that he be removed from its account. Fullenwider worked for Onward Technology, which provided IT support to Vineyard; the firm says technicians could reach client email but were not authorized to read it, and it fired him on May 11 after finding unauthorized access. Vineyard Mayor Zack Stratton told investigators that Fullenwider posted city emails to Facebook, including confidential attorney-client correspondence between the City Council and the city attorney. The Utah Attorney General's Office took up the case in May, and investigators say he accessed more than 700 emails.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump Gaza board pitches $2.45B Gaza plan, implementation uncertain
item.description: President Donald Trump's Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion plan Wednesday to begin rebuilding Gaza, presenting 66 programs to rehabilitate infrastructure and the economy at an event tied to the U.N. General Assembly. Officials conceded the plan's future is uncertain, with Israel and Hamas still at odds over terms of the U.S.-backed ceasefire announced nearly a year ago. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a long-term project that at least offers people hope. Jared Kushner, who devised the plan, acknowledged delays and said the effort was still sharpening the axe ahead of action. Reconstruction has yet to start as negotiators fail to agree on Hamas disarmament and Israeli withdrawal, leaving more than 2 million residents confined to about a third of the territory, and Israeli strikes continued Wednesday, killing four people including a Hamas official.
item.dc:creator: Nidal al-Mughrabi, Reuters

item.title: Mapleton bear removed from neighborhood
item.description: Utah wildlife officers trapped and removed a bear that had been raiding trash and feed in a Mapleton neighborhood for several weeks. Resident Cherise Rodman first saw the animal cross her driveway and get into garbage she had left out, and it returned the next day for a bag of chicken feed on her porch. Rodman keeps chickens and her neighbors have horses and other livestock, which she said made it lucky the bear never went after any animals. Neighbors kept storing cans in their garages, but the bear struck again Sunday night when the cans were left out, prompting the Utah Department of Wildlife to set a trap. The trap sprang Wednesday morning, and officers hauled the bear off without saying whether it would be killed or relocated.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: New Justice Court judge appointed; first new position in more than two decades
item.description: Nick Stiles has been appointed to the Salt Lake City Justice Court, filling a newly created sixth judgeship that is the court's first added position in more than 20 years. Mayor Erin Mendenhall selected Stiles from five forwarded candidates, and the City Council confirmed the choice Tuesday evening. Mendenhall said the court needed capacity to give cases proper attention and cited Stiles' range of experience across Utah's justice system. The court handles class B and C misdemeanors, infractions, traffic citations and small claims arising in Salt Lake City. Stiles currently administers the Utah Supreme Court and Court of Appeals, and previously worked as a city prosecutor, managed the Utah Judiciary's Domestic Violence Program and directed the Utah State Bar's Access to Justice Office.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Meta expected to unveil smart glasses without camera as privacy concerns grow
item.description: Meta was expected to introduce new smart glasses at its Connect conference Wednesday, including a camera-free pair, as scrutiny grows over AI devices that can record people without consent. The Information reported the camera-less models would come in two styles, Clubmaster and Burbank, alongside an expected refresh of the camera-equipped Meta Ray-Ban line and thinner augmented-reality glasses reportedly code-named Phoenix. Meta leads the category, with sales of the glasses it co-developed with EssilorLuxottica topping 7 million last year against mainly Chinese rivals such as RayNeo and Xiaomi. The devices have drawn restrictions at U.K. restaurants, pubs and theaters, plus a proposed California class action alleging Meta misled users about privacy and that human annotators reviewed footage of private moments; the company disputes the claims. Some analysts doubt dropping cameras resolves privacy worries, since the glasses can still capture audio.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Reuters

item.title: Provocative ad for bed sale leads to solicitation arrest
item.description: Miles Andrew Anderson, 22, of Salt Lake City, was arrested Tuesday and booked into the Salt Lake County Jail for investigation of 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor and obstruction of justice. The case began in June when a tipster reported a Craigslist listing that advertised a platform bed for $200 but included several photos of a girl, apparently about 12, posed on it in a nightgown. Salt Lake City police said the ad's wording and images were suspicious enough to open an investigation and obtain a warrant for the email address behind the post. Detectives traced the listing to Anderson and questioned him at his home. According to a booking affidavit, he initially claimed he had come across child sexual abuse material and bulk-downloaded it to make a predator-poaching post before deleting most of the files.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Award-winning author, creative writing teacher named Salt Lake City's first poet laureate
item.description: Poet and educator Joel Long has been named Salt Lake City's inaugural poet laureate by the city's Arts Council and Mayor's Office. Long, who lives in Sugar House, has taught English and creative writing at Rowland Hall since 2004 and has published seven books, five of them poetry collections. His honors include a White Pine Press Poetry Prize and a 2009 Salt Lake City Mayor's Award for Literary Arts. Mayor Erin Mendenhall said Long would help carry poetry beyond the page into daily city life while establishing the program's foundation. The three-year post, which drew 16 applicants after the search opened in April, carries a $5,000 annual honorarium and asks the laureate to write civic poems, run neighborhood readings and workshops, and develop a signature community project.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Space investment more than doubled to $23 billion in year to June, report says
item.description: Private investment in space companies worldwide more than doubled to $23 billion in the year through June, according to a report released Wednesday by British investment firm Seraphim and Relm Insurance. The firms attribute the surge partly to SpaceX's June IPO, which reshaped the funding landscape and drew investors hunting for the next comparable payoff. Relm said the sector is moving from hype to commercial reality, with capital flowing toward Earth observation, in-orbit manufacturing and satellite supply chains. Relm product development VP Andrew Bonwick said Earth observation's real value lies in analytics, since customers buy answers about ships, crops, refineries or wildfire risk rather than space services. The report found investors growing more selective toward Earth observation firms with visible revenue, while in-orbit manufacturing remains early-stage and satellite suppliers bring more production in-house to control costs.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram, Reuters

item.title: Lowe's employees give back to their community on Red Vest Day
item.description: Utah's Family Support Center was chosen earlier this year as one of 100 organizations nationwide to receive a Lowe's Community Impact Grant. On Tuesday, Lowe's Red Vest associates spent the morning at LifeStart Village in Midvale putting the $10,000 grant toward improvement projects for resident families. Kurt Baker, who manages a Lowe's in Layton, said employees live in the community and were glad for the chance to give back. LifeStart Village houses dozens of single-parent families working toward independence after domestic violence and homelessness. Staff say demand far outstrips capacity, with more than 400 families currently on the waiting list.
item.dc:creator: Allison Stuart, KSL

item.title: Polo off Mexican coast is among 'the strongest storms ever' as Odalys becomes a hurricane
item.description: Hurricane Polo, which the National Hurricane Center has called an extremely dangerous storm, was churning about 165 miles south of Zihuatanejo on Wednesday with maximum sustained winds of 150 mph after briefly reaching Category 5 strength. Forecasters expected it to turn sharply northwest and then west-northwest over several days, sparing land, though tropical storm conditions were anticipated in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima through Thursday. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts did not expect the storm to make landfall, but hurricane-force winds extended 40 miles from the center and tropical-storm winds up to 105 miles. Polo became the Pacific season's third Category 5 on Tuesday after Genevieve and Lowell. A second system, Odalys, strengthened Wednesday into a Category 1 hurricane roughly 1,295 miles off the southern tip of Baja California with no threat to land.
item.dc:creator: Megan Janetsky and Desiree Brooks, Associated Press

item.title: Actress, DNA expert to keynote next year's RootsTech. Tickets available now
item.description: RootsTech 2027 will run March 4-6 at the Salt Palace in downtown Salt Lake City under the theme "Celebrate!" — chosen to echo the Salt Lake Temple Celebration beginning a month after the conference. Organizers announced Wednesday that actress Jane Seymour and genetic genealogist CeCe Moore will deliver keynotes, with Moore speaking March 4 and Seymour March 5. Registration opened Wednesday at early bird pricing; online attendance, the expo hall and Family Discovery Day events remain free, while classes require paid registration. FamilySearch International, the family history arm of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, has hosted the conference for 16 years and drew participants from more than 200 countries in 2026 across events in 24 languages. FamilySearch events director Jonathan Wing said attendees are being invited to treat family history as a living celebration spanning past, present and future.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah cancer survivor completes Wasatch 100 with two of his sons
item.description: Cory Larrabee, 50, of Draper, finished this month's Wasatch 100 Endurance Run alongside his sons Keaton, 22, and McKay, 23. McKay said he stopped at mile 93 doubting he could beat the cutoff and asked his uncle for a blessing, which he credits as a major reason he finished. His father and brother had crossed hours earlier, and Cory was waiting at the line to embrace him. Cory first ran the race in 2002 with his own father, a year after finishing chemotherapy for cancer that cost him two of his four quadriceps muscles during his senior year as a track and cross-country athlete at Southern Utah University. He described that 2002 run as proof he could do hard things and the start of a new chapter, coming when Keaton was only a few months old.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Eagle Mountain rezoning for possible data center draws little opposition
item.description: A rezoning request that could eventually allow another data center in Eagle Mountain drew only two public comments at a planning commission hearing Tuesday night, a contrast to the heated debates such projects have triggered elsewhere in Utah. The proposal comes from property owner Reagan Peck, who holds 41 acres next to the existing Meta and QTS sites south of the city. Peck told the commission the request only changes zoning and does not guarantee a data center will be built. Meta has run its Eagle Mountain facility for about five years with roughly 1,200 employees, and the QTS campus due to finish in coming months is projected to add about 2,000 jobs. Economic Development Director Abby Ivory said residents have grown familiar with the technology and that the land has little other development potential, crediting the city's outreach for public trust.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Sandy among Utah communities set to celebrate 'Dolly Day'
item.description: Sandy will host a free outdoor screening of "Steel Magnolias" on Friday at Sandy City Hall in memory of Dolly Parton, who died Aug. 25 at 80. The date, dubbed "Dolly Day," nods to her 1980 hit "9 to 5," and Tremonton, Farmington, Park City and Cedar City are planning observances of their own. Mayor Monica Zoltanski said the singer had a knack for showing up in ways that mattered to people and fits Sandy's identity as a certified kindness city. Attendees are asked to bring a new children's book for the Canyons School District #CSDReads literacy campaign. Pinkbox Doughnuts is sponsoring the event, offering gift cards to the first 50 donors and a year of doughnuts to one.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake restaurant Monarca recognized by Mexican Consulate for quality, authenticity
item.description: The Mexican Consulate in Salt Lake City awarded downtown restaurant Monarca the Sello M, or M Seal, on Tuesday, making it the first Utah restaurant to earn the designation. Owners Alfonso and Claudia Brito opened the upscale restaurant in 2021 after building up from a taco cart to a food truck to their two Santo Taco taquerias in downtown and Rose Park. Acting general consul Antonio Cruz Diaz said the seal requires a rigorous evaluation showing a restaurant uses Mexican recipes, traditional ingredients and techniques, and cooks trained in authentic Mexican cuisine. He singled out Monarca's nixtamalization process for its tortillas, its Oaxacan corn, and its use of Utah-sourced products, saying the kitchen honors its roots while still innovating. The seal is part of a Mexican Foreign Ministry initiative that has recognized 38 other U.S. restaurants, including 17 around Los Angeles.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Friendly rivalry takes center stage at Salt Lake County Senior Decathlon
item.description: Nearly 100 older adults gathered Tuesday at the Magna Kennecott Senior Center for Salt Lake County's annual Senior Decathlon. Participants from senior centers across the county competed in 10 games and activities alongside live music and food. Reigning champion Sherry Mousley, who says she once won three gold medals at a single decathlon, sat out the competition this year. Instead she volunteered, running the Boggle station, and joked that she already had enough medals. Mousley said the senior center remains a central part of her life regardless of whether she is competing.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake City close to fully replacing 200 North Temple trees lost in 2024 mishap
item.description: Salt Lake City is roughly halfway through replacing the hundreds of trees a city worker accidentally killed along the North Temple corridor in 2024 by spraying them with herbicide. Public Lands crews began planting 100 new trees in August and are repairing irrigation and soil for another 100 that have waited in planters since the mishap, with completion expected by the end of November, according to deputy director Tyler Murdock. Another 30 to 40 trees are slated for 1000 West in Fairpark this year through a partnership with the Utah State Fairpark, part of some 270 additional trees planned near the corridor along with hundreds of rose bushes. The original plantings dated to UTA's green line TRAX construction, which opened in 2013. Fairpark Community Council chairman Jeffery Olson said neighbors were distraught as the trees died off.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: 'You will not receive forgiveness from me,' sister of DUI victim tells former Layton officer
item.description: Samuel Andrew Rockwell, a former Layton police officer, appeared before the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole on Tuesday for the first time since his conviction in the 2021 crash that killed 23-year-old Emily Worley. Rockwell was off duty but already suspended and facing termination when he crashed on Bangerter Highway at an estimated 116 mph; he pleaded guilty in 2023 to automobile homicide while driving under the influence and drew a one-to-15-year sentence. Worley's sister, Kaitlin Krulisky, told the board she would not forgive him, saying he had sworn an oath to protect lives. Her father, Richard Krulisky, argued two years was too little and objected that Rockwell has served his time in county jails rather than state prison. The family also took issue with his law enforcement and military service having been raised at sentencing as grounds for leniency.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah Youth Sports Giving Day close to $4 million in overall donations
item.description: Utah Youth Sports Giving Day has drawn nearly $2.4 million in donations less than two weeks after launching, and matching gifts from Utah businesses and foundations push the campaign's total impact toward $4 million. The first-year effort targets cost, which organizers call one of the biggest barriers keeping Utah children out of sports. Jenny Teemsma of Miller Sports + Entertainment said the state calls itself the state of sport and wants young families to have access to it. Utah Crew head coach Victoria Rojo said rowing carries high operating costs and that the money lets her program expand scholarships and cut dues. The campaign, led by Miller Sports + Entertainment with the Larry H. & Gail Miller Family Foundation and the Daniels Fund, opened Sept. 12 at a Salt Lake Bees game and passed its $1 million public goal in under 10 minutes.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
item.description: Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials announced Tuesday plans to strip 760,000 people from Affordable Care Act exchanges, alleging the enrollments were fraudulent or tied to people who do not exist. Vance, who leads a government anti-fraud task force, said canceling roughly 315,000 enrollments covering those 760,000 individuals would save $2.2 billion, and he faulted the government for not verifying eligibility. He appeared alongside CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz and said another 419,000 enrollments face additional eligibility checks. The administration also imposed a six-month freeze on new agents and brokers signing up enrollees, saying that group accounts for a disproportionate share of the fraud identified. About 19.2 million Americans were enrolled in ACA marketplace plans as of early 2026, a figure that grew during the pandemic under enhanced subsidies from laws signed by former President Joe Biden.
item.dc:creator: Fatima Hussein & Michelle Price, Associated Press

item.title: 2 outdoor hockey rinks now open for public use in St. George
item.description: St. George has opened two outdoor rinks at JC Snow Park near downtown, built not for ice but for ball hockey, and they are free for public use as park amenities. Cory Henwood, who heads Red Rock Hockey, said the sport has grown fast locally and his organization offered the city both money and labor to improve and expand the space. The league began in 2023 with 50 players practicing in a school parking lot, then moved to an outdoor futsal field at the same park while hauling in its own boards. Growth to several hundred participants drove the push for a purpose-built venue. Henwood said Red Rock Hockey helped channel donations well into the six figures toward building the new rink and refurbishing the existing one.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Meta, Utah Valley University partnering to build observatory in Eagle Mountain
item.description: Meta has given Utah Valley University $450,000 toward building the Walden Park Observatory in Eagle Mountain, raising the company's total contribution to the project to $700,000. UVU, Utah County and the city of Eagle Mountain have also chipped in, and the site sits at Walden Park on North Frontier Street. UVU physics professor Joe Jensen stressed that the facility is meant for public access rather than research, deliberately sited in town instead of on a remote dark-sky peak. Jensen said the building will also host lectures for UVU students and faculty, and its design departs from the domed shape most people picture because a conventional dome would not have suited the surrounding neighborhood.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Utah History Summit brings historians together to expand the state's story
item.description: Historians, museum staff and community organizations from around Utah are meeting at the Museum of Utah for the first Utah History Summit. The gathering focuses on how state history gets preserved and shared, and on widening which communities are represented in that record. Eliza Carr, public programming manager for the Utah Historical Society, said organizers want to spotlight history work happening across Utah. One effort highlighted is the Peoples of Utah Revisited Project, which builds on a 1976 bicentennial book in which each chapter examined a different Utah demographic that had not previously been researched.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: False bomb threat causes road closures in West Haven
item.description: A reported bomb threat in West Haven on Tuesday turned out to be false after an extended police response that shut down part of 1900 West. Weber County Sheriff's Lt. Sean Endsley said the report came in around 9 a.m. and that both northbound and southbound lanes between 2550 South and 2100 South were closed while crews worked. Nearby businesses were evacuated as a bomb squad and K-9 units from Davis County swept the area. Nothing was found, but Endsley said investigators will follow up on the origin of the threat.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Exclusive-Meta testing a 'human concierge' for its new personal AI agent, Muse
item.description: Internal company posts reviewed by Reuters show Meta has been piloting a “human concierge” arrangement in which contractors quietly take over some phone calls placed by its new AI assistant, Muse. Meta told employees about the test last week, shortly after publicly launching Muse's calling feature. Muse, which has led U.S. app download charts since debuting two weeks ago, is built to carry out tasks on a user's behalf such as sending email, shopping and booking travel, and the calling feature lets it phone U.S. businesses to book appointments, check stock or gather contractor quotes. According to the posts, some employees objected on privacy grounds, warning that routing calls through call-center contractors could expose sensitive user information unintentionally.
item.dc:creator: Katie Paul, Reuters

item.title: Italian police find $3.6 million in cash hidden in apartment's walls, floors and furniture
item.description: Italian anti-mafia officers recovered $3.6 million in cash concealed in the walls, floors and furniture of an apartment in Caivano, near Naples, during a dawn raid Monday that produced 34 arrests. The Naples Carabinieri told CNN the money was in bundles of 50-euro notes wrapped in cellophane and stacked beneath floor and wall tiles and inside hidden wardrobe drawers, and officers hauled it out in plastic mop buckets to an armored vehicle. Police also seized 11 Rolex watches along with weapons and drug-dealing paraphernalia. Anti-mafia prosecutor Nicola Gratteri, who led the months-long operation, said investigators wiretapped cellphones that relatives had smuggled to incarcerated mobsters. Gratteri told reporters that a single home yielded 3.2 million euros in cash plus the valuable watches.
item.dc:creator: Barbie Latza Nadeau, CNN

item.title: Category 5 Hurricane Polo is an 'extremely dangerous' storm off the coast of Mexico
item.description: Hurricane Polo strengthened into a Category 5 storm off Mexico's southwestern coast on Tuesday and was expected to intensify further, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. Forecasters described it as extremely dangerous with maximum sustained winds of 165 mph, centered about 205 miles south of Zihuatanejo and stationary over the Pacific at midday, and said an aircraft would be flown into the storm to gather data. Mexican authorities suspended classes in several coastal areas as the system brushed the shoreline. Forecasters warned of flash flooding and mudslides, with 3 to 6 inches of rain expected in Guerrero and Michoacán and lesser amounts along coastal Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco. Guerrero and Oaxaca have been hit by several powerful hurricanes in recent years and some communities are still recovering.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Semitruck driver accused of driving on I-15 shoulder without valid license
item.description: Irune Alonso Heredia, 35, of Des Plaines, Illinois, was arrested Monday and charged Tuesday in 4th District Court after allegedly driving a semitruck erratically on I-15. Prosecutors filed reckless endangerment, a third-degree felony carrying a road rage enhancement, along with a class C misdemeanor for operating a commercial vehicle without a commercial driver's license. The Utah Highway Patrol said it received reports of a semi weaving across the road around 4:50 p.m., with at least three drivers calling in, and charging documents say the truck passed a vehicle on the right shoulder. A trooper stopped the semi near Nephi and noted the trailer was still resting on the white line. According to the arrest affidavit, the driver angrily questioned why she had been pulled over before the trooper could speak.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah firefighters begin prescribed burns as preventative measure
item.description: Crews have started prescribed burning in the Heber-Kamas Ranger District, concentrating on the Castle Peak area. Firefighters are also working in the Pitt and Page area, where smoke will likely be visible to nearby residents. Dispatchers asked the public not to call in reports of smoke from these planned operations. Crews burned roughly 1,300 slash piles over the weekend, each pile being a gathered stack of forest debris that firefighters ignite in a single controlled spot.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI
item.description: The extortion group ShinyHunters claims it breached the FBI and stole data on thousands of bureau employees. In a statement on its dark-web site and in an online chat with Reuters, the group said it targeted the FBI in retaliation for a May 2026 bureau announcement that described ShinyHunters' techniques and urged targets not to pay. The group provided what it said was a screenshot of a defaced FBI job site plus a sample of stolen data; Reuters could not verify the screenshot, though a notice on the FBI job site Tuesday said it and the Special Agent Applicant Portal were unavailable. Reuters partially corroborated some of the personnel information by checking names and addresses against credit bureau records and previously breached data held by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs. The FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens, Reuters

item.title: Aircraft company identifies 2nd pilot killed in Yosemite helicopter firefighting crash
item.description: Contract operator Precision identified the second pilot killed in Sunday's firefighting helicopter crash in Yosemite National Park as Ryan Cutter, 46, a Utah pilot who lived in Park City. Cutter and pilot Greg King, both Precision employees, were the only people aboard the AS332 Super Puma when it went down near Ostrander Lake shortly before 2 p.m. while conducting water drops on a wildfire in the park. The lake lies about 9 miles south of El Capitan and roughly 7 miles northeast of Wawona. Precision said in a social media post accompanying photos of the two pilots that they brought honor to the mission and would not be forgotten. The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate, and first responders held a procession honoring Cutter on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Boone, Associated Press

item.title: New York airport operations resume after disruptions across Northeast due to technical problems
item.description: Flights resumed at New York City-area airports on Tuesday with lingering delays and cancellations after damaged communications lines at an FAA facility in Philadelphia were repaired. The primary line failed Monday and the backup fiber optic line was accidentally cut by railroad construction crews, leaving controllers without radar or communications for hours and nearly halting commercial traffic. More than 600 flights into and out of Newark Liberty International were canceled Monday, part of hundreds scrubbed across the Northeast as every major New York-area airport was affected. Flightaware.com showed roughly 40 delays and close to 60 cancellations at Newark early Tuesday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said online that clearing the backlog would still take time.
item.dc:creator: Josh Funk, Associated Press

item.title: Public invited to official lighting of new outdoor art in Syracuse
item.description: Syracuse will hold a lighting ceremony this week for a newly installed bison sculpture called Colossus of Growing Prosperity. The piece was unveiled over the weekend at the roundabout near 1950 S. 3000 West. City officials said the design draws on Syracuse's ties to the Great Salt Lake and Antelope Island, with the bison meant to convey strength, energy and community growth. The public is invited to the ceremony Thursday, Sept. 24, at Fire Station 31 beginning at 8 p.m.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Banned White House outlets cover Trump at UN as court hearing looms
item.description: Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico covered President Donald Trump's appearance at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday using U.N.-issued credentials, days after he barred the three outlets from the White House grounds. Entering the U.N. building, Trump told reporters he was surprised CNN was there and said the network should not be, referencing a claim that it would stop covering him; CNN has not said any such thing. Trump announced the ban Friday on social media, writing that the outlets should not be able to report what he called fiction and lies about the president, and defended the move again Monday. The three organizations sued Trump and administration officials Monday, arguing the ban violates First Amendment protections for speech and the press. They are seeking a temporary restraining order in federal court in Washington, with a hearing set for Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Helen Coster, Reuters

item.title: Lawsuits allege Ozempic, other GLP-1 medications may cause sudden vision loss
item.description: Lawsuits filed against the makers of GLP-1 drugs including Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound claim the medications may be connected to nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, a rare optic nerve disorder that causes abrupt vision loss. One woman who had been taking a GLP-1 for weight loss said she woke up one morning unable to see out of her right eye; she works as a nurse practitioner and said she can no longer read, affecting her ability to work. Hundreds of other Americans have also sued, arguing they were not adequately warned about the risk. The drugmakers reject the allegations and say there is no evidence their products caused the vision loss.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Agent Orange memorial in Sunset sought by Syracuse Vietnam War veteran largely complete
item.description: A monument honoring people harmed by Agent Orange is nearly finished at Sunset City Veterans Memorial Park, the result of a years-long push by Syracuse resident and Air Force veteran Larry Kerr. Workers set the last of the large black marble panels on Monday, including one inscribed with the line about being wounded by dioxin and honored by all. Kerr, who attributes his own cancers and heart disease to Agent Orange exposure during his Vietnam service, calls it the largest memorial of its kind in the country. A formal dedication is expected closer to Veterans Day on Nov. 11. Kerr is pressing to finish the remaining steps as he deals with new medical findings of his own.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Major name in US politics coming to Utah
item.description: Former U.S. House Speaker Paul Ryan will give the keynote address at the 2027 Utah Economic Outlook and Public Policy Summit, set for Jan. 14 at the Grand America Hotel in Salt Lake City. The Utah Chamber and the University of Utah's Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute announced the booking. Ryan represented Wisconsin in Congress and led the House as speaker from October 2015 through January 2019, and he was Mitt Romney's running mate in the 2012 presidential race against Barack Obama. Organizers said his talk will center on free enterprise, economic policy and the business climate in Utah. The summit gathers business, policy and academic figures to discuss the state's economic outlook ahead of the legislative session.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Trump says Iran deal nearing, Tehran offers Hormuz reopening
item.description: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Washington and Tehran were moving toward a settlement, while a senior Iranian official indicated Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the U.S. eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports. Trump spoke after meeting British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations, saying Iran has been talking to the U.S. and the relationship is developing, but that Iran cannot be allowed a nuclear weapon. He offered no specifics, and no face-to-face meetings between the two governments are known to have occurred since July, when an interim agreement to end the war collapsed weeks after being signed. His remarks came hours after a combative General Assembly speech in which he repeated a threat to annihilate Iran absent a deal and called for its complete economic isolation.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery, Parisa Hafezi and Antoni Slodkowski, Reuters

item.title: Wall Street expects Meta's AI agent to shape into a new revenue engine
item.description: Analysts have grown bullish on Meta Platforms on expectations that its AI agent Muse will become a fresh revenue stream and change how the company monetizes AI. Muse launched Sept. 8 and can handle tasks such as sending email, booking travel and completing transactions, offered free in a basic tier with paid plans at $20 and $100 a month. Meta shares have climbed more than 20% since the launch, outpacing the other large-cap tech names and adding over $200 billion in market value to reach a seven-month high; the stock rose 0.5% Tuesday after an 11% jump the prior session. J.P. Morgan analysts wrote that Muse could become the most widely used consumer AI application since ChatGPT, pointing to product-market fit, Meta's distribution and a free tier that makes trial easy.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Chauhan, Reuters

item.title: Corporate bond buyers get picky with flood of AI debt
item.description: The high-grade corporate credit market has bifurcated, with investors bidding eagerly for bonds from traditional financial and industrial issuers while treating AI-linked debt cautiously. Portfolio managers say the concern is not default risk at hyperscalers but the scale and unpredictability of borrowing needed for data centers, chips and AI infrastructure, which has them demanding larger concessions and revisiting concentration limits. Goldman Sachs data show hyperscaler gross issuance is projected to reach a record $420 billion next year, up 60% from 2026 estimates, against overall U.S. corporate issuance of $1.9 trillion through August, a 30% year-over-year rise per SIFMA. Colby Stilson, head of fixed income at Brown Advisory in London, said his firm is being very selective within hyperscaler debt.
item.dc:creator: Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Reuters

item.title: Missing man found in partially submerged minivan in Box Elder County
item.description: Lewis “Lou” Balzomo, 66, who was the subject of a Silver Alert after last being seen Thursday, was found dead Sunday inside a green Toyota Sienna partly submerged in a canal near Fielding. Box Elder County Chief Deputy Sheriff Cade Palmer announced the discovery in a Facebook post, crediting the sheriff's office, the county search and rescue team and a SCUBA team for the recovery. Investigators believe Balzomo missed a right-hand turn, drove through a field and went down a steep 70-foot embankment into the canal. Palmer offered condolences to Balzomo's family and thanked the people who shared the original alert and helped search. The crash remained under investigation Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: St. George's gas average pushes past $5 per gallon. Is the state next?
item.description: AAA's gas price index put the St. George metro area just above $5 for a gallon of regular on Tuesday, making it the first of Utah's five tracked metros to cross that line in the current run-up. Logan, Ogden, Provo-Orem and Salt Lake City averages sat between $4.92 and $4.94, with the statewide figure near $4.96. Several counties had already passed $5, topped by Piute County at $5.34 and including Beaver, Duchesne, Grand, San Juan, Summit and Washington, while neighboring Garfield County was lowest at $4.89. Premium averaged $5.48 and diesel $6.56, both state records per the index. Analysts attribute the climb largely to elevated crude oil prices.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Zelenskyy to meet Trump at UN in push for energy truce with Russia
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was scheduled to meet President Donald Trump at the United Nations in New York on Tuesday to press for a truce covering energy infrastructure. Ukrainians worry Russia is preparing to strike heating and power facilities this winter after escalating aerial attacks by both sides that have damaged ports, warehouses, ships and energy sites and hampered Black Sea exports. Zelenskyy wrote on X on Monday that Ukraine's energy sector, critical infrastructure and food exports must stop being targets, and that matching de-escalation steps would follow. He had cited diplomatic momentum after a Sunday phone call with Trump, though Russia, which holds a missile advantage, has given no indication it wants to pause the air campaign. Trump, whose approval ratings have hit a record low amid high gas prices before November's midterms, has voiced concern about damage to Russian oil refineries.
item.dc:creator: Tom Balmforth, Reuters

item.title: Trump, Greenland, Denmark sign deal in bid to end Arctic standoff
item.description: President Donald Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement Tuesday during the U.N. General Assembly allowing an expanded U.S. military presence on Greenland, potentially defusing a standoff over the mineral-rich Arctic island. The deal stops short of Trump's demand that the United States absorb Greenland as a territory to counter Russian and Chinese activity in the Arctic, an outcome Greenlandic leaders resisted. Text released after the signing permits the U.S. to build a “Golden Dome” ballistic missile defense system on the island, which sits on the shortest route between Europe and North America and hosts the northernmost U.S. military base. In his speech before the ceremony, Trump characterized the agreement as giving the U.S. permanent control over security and other needs there.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen, Reuters

item.title: 'You should be ashamed': Park City councilman walks out during meeting on park wall
item.description: A Park City councilman left Thursday's council meeting partway through after colleagues took a different direction than he wanted on a concrete wall at City Park. The dispute came up under the final agenda item, when the recreation department sought guidance on the design of a basketball court wall at The Mine, the rebuilt community center at 1400 Sullivan Road slated to open in December. The 8-foot wall separating the playground from the court was part of the approved plans, but residents have objected to its size and the way it blocks views now that it is standing. A city staff report acknowledged the wall reads as more imposing in person than in the renderings while defending the design as intentional, meant to give the court a defined edge.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: AI infrastructure firm Accelevation targets up to $5.4 billion valuation in US IPO
item.description: Data center infrastructure company Accelevation said Tuesday it is seeking a valuation as high as $5.37 billion in its U.S. initial public offering. The Miamisburg, Ohio-based firm and some existing shareholders aim to raise up to $720 million by selling 30 million shares priced between $20 and $24. The autumn IPO window opened cautiously amid rising bond yields and the first U.S. interest-rate increase in three years, but a queue of prominent issuers suggests activity is picking up: Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Nscale filed this month, smart-ring maker Oura began its roadshow this week, and Anthropic is preparing a possible large listing later this year. Kat Liu, a vice president at research firm IPOX, said investors will grow more selective as choices multiply, weighing where a company sits in the value chain and the quality of its backlog.
item.dc:creator: Pragyan Kalita, Reuters

item.title: Moab woman shot last week dies from injuries
item.description: Moab police said Tuesday that Anzhela “Angela” Pronina, 33, died Monday afternoon from gunshot wounds she suffered on Sept. 15. Police say Charles Anthony “Tony” Nelson, 30, shot her at her home on West Williams Way and then killed himself. Pronina had been flown by medical helicopter in extremely critical condition to a hospital that authorities did not name. Police said she was an organ donor and that once doctors concluded she would not survive, her organs were recovered for transplant; Chief Lex Bell called that her final gift and extended condolences to her family in Moab and in Ukraine. Investigators are still conducting interviews, including with relatives in Ukraine, and expect to release more details next week.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: New justice center could be in Davis County's future
item.description: Davis County commissioners received a Sept. 1 proposal to consolidate county attorney offices and a new courthouse into a single justice center. County court operations are currently split among aging courthouses in Farmington, Bountiful and Layton, and a county project document says all three have security shortcomings and none meets current standards for safety, accessibility or capacity. The document argues that running three buildings costs taxpayers more, scatters services and leaves those security gaps unaddressed. The proposed five-story, 179,296-square-foot building carries a $171.2 million price tag, of which Davis County would cover $29.2 million. The plan also contemplates a state contribution paid through an annual appropriation over 20 to 30 years, plus revenue from a new county sales tax.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Bipartisan bill aims to expand health protections for wildland firefighters
item.description: Following one of Utah's worst recent wildfire seasons, lawmakers from both parties in the House and Senate are backing the proposed Wildland Firefighter Health and Safety Act. Supporters say it would direct new resources toward the long-term health risks crews face as wildfires grow more frequent and intense. Timothy Ingalsbee, executive director of Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics and Ecology, noted that vehicle and aircraft accidents claimed lives this summer while many young firefighters carry illnesses and injuries they may not recognize until years later. His group has endorsed the bill, which would establish a task force and an advisory council staffed by wildland firefighters to shape policies reducing workplace injury and illness. Ingalsbee said the central aim is early detection.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: 2 men charged in car loan fraud scheme
item.description: Yonder Jesus Reyes-Zabala, 25, and Jose Miguel Espinoza Araujo, 23, were charged Monday in 3rd District Court with communications fraud, a second-degree felony, plus third-degree felony counts of forgery and possession of a forged writing. Herriman police were called to a credit union on Sept. 15 for a suspected fraud in progress and found the two men waiting in the lobby. Charging documents say Espinoza had applied that morning for a $41,000 title loan to buy a 2025 Ford Explorer. The pair allegedly tried to withdraw the full amount, getting $15,000 at the Herriman branch and $10,000 at Riverton before the Draper branch sent them back over an irregularity flagged on the account. Investigators have indicated the case may be linked to another recent arrest.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'We lost our house': A deadly standoff left homes riddled with bullets. Who pays for the damage?
item.description: In June 2025, Cache County deputies responding to a call at the Valley View Mobile Home Park in Hyrum came under gunfire from Jorge Andrade, who had just killed his wife, Holly Andrade, and who authorities say was wearing what appeared to be a homemade explosive vest. Body camera and doorbell recordings captured him firing sporadically through the neighborhood as responders called for backup, and Cache County Chief Deputy Mikelshan Bartschi described the scene as extremely high risk. Resident RaeAnn Bott can be heard on a 911 recording reporting continued shooting. Both Jorge and Holly Andrade were found dead hours later inside their home. The KSL report examines who bears the cost of repairing neighboring homes left riddled with bullets after the standoff.
item.dc:creator: Daniella Rivera, KSL

item.title: Palo Alto Networks unveils AI-powered cybersecurity service using Claude, GPT models
item.description: Palo Alto Networks said Tuesday it will launch a business cybersecurity service built on advanced AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to surface vulnerabilities across corporate systems. The offering, called Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, draws on cyber-focused models including Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Cyber along with open-weight models. It is designed to continuously probe web applications, APIs and cloud infrastructure so customers can spot weaknesses and likely attack paths as their environments shift, and it also recommends fixes including code-level changes and virtual patching. The company said the service will be sold globally via annual subscriptions priced according to the mix of models used. Palo Alto framed the product as a response to attackers increasingly using AI to find and exploit gaps in corporate networks.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Colorado State apologizes after derogatory 'Mormon' chants during BYU football game
item.description: Colorado State University apologized after derogatory chants aimed at members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints came from portions of its student section during Saturday's football game against BYU. In a statement issued during the game, the school said mocking anyone's faith has no place at CSU, apologized to BYU's players, fans and church members, and said the behavior conflicts with the university's values. The statement added that administrators are addressing the incident with students. Longtime BYU fan Daniel Jensen said the chanting started before kickoff and recurred throughout the night, and that it involved a large number of students rather than a few individuals.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Taylor Frankie Paul announces exit from 'The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives'
item.description: Taylor Frankie Paul said Monday that she is leaving “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” ahead of Season 6 filming, tying the decision to developments in her custody disputes. She is negotiating custody with former boyfriend Dakota Mortensen, with whom she has one son, and with ex-husband Tate Paul, with whom she shares a son and a daughter. In July she checked herself into a rehab facility after months of public fallout from a since-closed police investigation into an alleged domestic abuse incident involving Mortensen. In her social media statement she thanked the networks that supported her and gave her a chance to return, while saying she did not want to continue under the current circumstances and addressing her strained relationships with castmates.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby, Deseret News

item.title: 10 years later, man sentenced to prison for role in teen's shooting death over thrown egg
item.description: Third District Judge Elizabeth Hruby-Mills sentenced Martin Antonio Cruz, now 31, on Monday to one to 15 years in prison for manslaughter, a second-degree felony, with credit for the more than nine years he has already spent in jail. The case stems from the July 5, 2016, killing of 16-year-old Paris Gustin, who charging documents say was shot while inside a Honda after an egging; prosecutors alleged Cruz and Fortunato Nato Villagrana used an AK-47. Ashley Gustin, the teen's mother, spoke at the hearing alongside other relatives and said she had sensed that morning that her son was gone. She told the court she struggled to find words for what had been done to her and her son, saying the killing destroyed her as well. Gustin also said she saw no emotion or remorse from Cruz.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Davis County students run for shelter during hail storm, tornado warning after early release
item.description: Davis School District students are still shaken after Friday's severe weather struck just after early dismissal. Elementary schools in the district release at 1:30 p.m. on Fridays, and a tornado warning for Davis County followed at 1:45 p.m., with rain, hail and wind arriving in the minutes beforehand. Many children were outside or walking home when hail described as the size of ping-pong or golf balls began falling. Hill Field Elementary Assistant Principal Jessica Miller said parents and students crowded into the hallway and that she comforted one boy crying hysterically who had been struck in the head by hail before anyone understood what had hit him. Miller said staff scrambled to get students to safety.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: 'Great for our water supply': BYU study examines how rock glaciers fit into Utah's water puzzle
item.description: The Utah Geological Survey, Brigham Young University and other Utah institutions are jointly studying rock glaciers, slow-moving masses of ice and rock debris that store water and release it gradually long after seasonal snow has melted. One such formation on Mount Timpanogos feeds Emerald Lake near the summit. BYU geology professor Greg Carling said in a video that a rock glacier resembles a pile of rocks but moves downhill much as an ice glacier does. Because Utah draws roughly 95% of its water from snowpack, researchers see these formations as a meaningful piece of the state's supply picture. BYU geology graduate student Lerato Thoka-Cole said they are becoming a major water source.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: How the Davis County tornado dispelled a common weather myth
item.description: A tornado that touched down near Francis Peak on Friday cut a swath of downed and snapped trees roughly 100 to 200 yards wide and more than a mile long. KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson, who visited the site Saturday, said the scarred and tangled trees indicated substantial wind carrying heavy debris. The National Weather Service's Salt Lake City office is still assessing damage and may not rate the tornado's strength until next week. The same system dropped quarter- and half-dollar-sized hail across several Davis County communities, and a landspout touched down about 15 miles southeast of Naples in Uintah County. National Weather Service lead meteorologist Christine Kruse said mountain tornadoes are not as unusual as people assume, undercutting a persistent myth.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Alcohol use has declined for the first time since Covid-19, with Gen Zers and millennials leading the charge
item.description: A study published Monday in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that alcohol use among U.S. adults, including heavy drinking, fell between 2022 and 2024, though rates remain above where they stood in 2018. Lead author Dr. Brian P. Lee, a hepatologist and liver transplant specialist at Keck Medicine of USC, drew on cross-sectional data covering more than 114,000 people from 2018 through 2024. Lee said the pandemic drove a surge in drinking in 2020 that had not eased two years later, and that he saw waiting rooms fill with liver disease patients, including people in their 20s needing transplants, a pattern absent before 2020. He called the first decline a reason for hope while cautioning that a single change does not establish a lasting trend.
item.dc:creator: Avni Trivedi, CNN

item.title: Swig's 'Save the Cups' campaign aims to raise $650K for women battling breast cancer
item.description: Swig locations are running the company's annual “Save the Cups” campaign through Oct. 10, with a goal of raising $650,000 to help women manage the financial side of breast cancer treatment. Founder Nicole Robison started the effort out of personal experience, having been diagnosed with a rare form of breast cancer at 37, a year before launching Swig. Robison said the money pressures often get overlooked next to the physical and emotional toll, noting that medical bills keep arriving while patients are too sick from chemotherapy and radiation to want to burden their families. Carrie McKee, who bought a drink and donated to the campaign in 2021, later found herself on the receiving end of that help.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Utah boy gets cancer-free surprise at Fairpark's demolition derby
item.description: Silas Anderson, a 12-year-old who was recently declared cancer-free, was the VIP guest Saturday night at the Utah State Fairpark's “Day of Wreckoning” demolition derby. Before the event he and his family toured the pits and met drivers, and he rode into the arena for the national anthem. Afterward Make-A-Wish Utah revealed that his wish for a family trip to Hawaii had been granted, funded through a Chartway Promise Foundation grant. Make-A-Wish Utah president and CEO Daniel Dudley described Silas as brave and adventurous. Silas was diagnosed with stage four adenocarcinoma at age 10, a cancer his father Travis Anderson said is usually found in babies.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: The school day ends before the workday. Utah parents are feeling the gap
item.description: Afterschool Alliance data cited in the Utah After 3 p.m. report shows parents of 348,357 Utah children would enroll them in an afterschool program if one existed, but roughly five in six of those children — 290,465 — are not in one. Only 57,892 Utah children participated in 2025. Ben Trentelman, who leads the Utah Afterschool Network, said the shortage of programs is the single biggest barrier, with rural areas short on programs and transportation while urban areas have too many children chasing too few slots. Families without options lean on older siblings, grandparents, relatives or neighbors, and some children are left unsupervised for about six to six and a half hours a week between 3 and 5 p.m.
item.dc:creator: Aleigha Marie McDonough, KSL

item.title: Provo police identify man shot, killed by officers over the weekend
item.description: Provo police named Dillon James Wright, 31, as the man two officers shot and killed Saturday night in a parking lot near 2230 N. University Parkway. Officers were dispatched about 9:15 p.m. to a reported domestic violence assault in progress, and the woman involved told them Wright had a gun. Police said both officers fired and struck him, but have not yet said what prompted the shooting or whether Wright was armed at that moment. Wright died of his injuries at Utah Valley Hospital, and the officers were placed on standard paid administrative leave. The Utah County Officer-Involved Critical Incident team is investigating.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Here's how Utah's higher education system can grapple with a declining college-age population
item.description: New projections show Utah's population of 18- to 24-year-olds will keep growing only through 2028 before falling for close to two decades, ending the demographic tailwind that drove a decade of enrollment growth. A report from the University of Utah's Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute lays out how institutions can adapt to that shift. Lead author Heidi Prior, a senior public policy analyst at the institute, said the coming decline reflects a broader change in the state's age structure with real consequences for higher education. The report also points to eroding public confidence as a separate pressure, citing a 2025 Lumina Foundation-Gallup survey in which 42% of Americans expressed confidence in higher education, down from 57% a decade earlier, and a Pew finding that about seven in 10 think U.S. higher education is headed the wrong direction.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Arrest made in Sandy shooting investigation
item.description: Sandy police arrested Carl Devon Hardy, 30, on Sunday in connection with a shooting near 8400 S. State Street that wounded a man in the foot. He was booked for investigation of aggravated assault resulting in serious injury, illegal discharge of a gun, being a restricted person in possession of a gun and drug paraphernalia use. According to a booking affidavit, two men in their 20s told investigators a confrontation with people from a nearby apartment balcony escalated after they left and returned, at which point someone emerged from the complex and opened fire. The wounded man and his companion fled into a canal behind a gas station and were later found by Unified police. Detectives said license plate reader data placed Hardy's vehicle eastbound on I-80 toward Evanston, Wyoming, about an hour after the shooting, and determined he was not in a vehicle when he fired.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Man who attacked officer while trying to escape custody given prison time
item.description: Sergio Lopez Ramirez, 43, was sentenced to zero to five years in prison on each of two third-degree felonies after pleading guilty to assault by prisoner and property damage. Charging documents say that in June of last year, while Adult Probation and Parole agents were delivering him to the Salt Lake County Jail and stepped out to deal with malfunctioning gates, Lopez slipped his handcuffs to the front of his body and broke out the patrol car's rear window, cutting one agent's cornea with flying glass. His Aug. 14 plea deal dropped an attempted aggravated escape charge and reduced the original first- and second-degree felony counts. The terms run concurrently with each other and with anything else he is serving, and he received credit for 415 days already served. Court records show prior convictions including a 2015 West Valley City incident in which an officer fell 10 feet from a strip mall roof while trying to arrest him.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: 'Kind of scary': Pineview visitors discover grenade on previously submerged reservoir shore
item.description: Two brothers bow fishing at a drained Pineview Reservoir on Sunday found a rusted grenade along the rocky bank near the dam on the reservoir's west end. Landen Waite of Clinton said he initially picked it up thinking it was a downrigger fishing weight before spotting the pin; he and his brother Conner set it down and alerted a dam official. The Weber County Sheriff's Office Bomb Squad detonated the device in place Sunday evening with no injuries, according to Sgt. Danielle Goodell. Conner Waite said the exposed lakebed held “all kinds of old junk,” including a cut-apart safe, in an area that looked untouched for years. The low water level that drew them to the spot has been steadily uncovering items long hidden beneath the surface.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Intoxicated driver arrested in hit-and-run crash with pedestrian in Utah County
item.description: Gabriel Fulgencio, 23, of Santaquin, was booked into the Utah County Jail on Sunday for investigation of negligently operating a vehicle causing serious injury, leaving the scene of an injury accident, DUI, drug possession and paraphernalia use. Utah County sheriff's deputies were called Sunday morning to 3100 West and 7300 South, where a man walking on the road had been struck by a black Ram pickup that did not stop; the pedestrian was hospitalized in critical condition. A deputy spotted a black pickup with front-end damage nearby and pulled it over. According to the booking affidavit, Fulgencio said he may have hit something but kept driving because he was scared, and told police he had stopped drinking around 4 a.m. A breath test put his blood-alcohol level at 0.139%, nearly three times the legal limit.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Smart ring maker Oura eyes $15.6 billion IPO valuation in fall listings demand test
item.description: Oura began the roadshow for its U.S. initial public offering on Monday, aiming at a fully diluted valuation of $15.62 billion. The smart ring maker and some existing shareholders would raise as much as $2.2 billion by selling 50 million shares at the top of an indicated $40 to $44 range, with the listing expected next week. Eli Lilly has signaled interest in buying up to $100 million of shares and investment firm Dragoneer up to $300 million. Samuel Kerr, global head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, called the deal the first real test of U.S. appetite after a sluggish September, saying a strong debut would encourage other issuers while a weak one would suggest sentiment is turning. The offering comes as markets contend with uncertainty over AI valuations, rising bond yields and a shifting Federal Reserve outlook.
item.dc:creator: Manya Saini, Reuters

item.title: How much would the Great Salt Lake benefit without phragmites?
item.description: Keith Hambrecht, restoration and invasive species program manager for the Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands, told the Utah Legislative Water Development Commission on Thursday that clearing invasive phragmites could help the Great Salt Lake hold tens of thousands of additional acre-feet of water each year. He showed lawmakers a 2003 photo of Farmington Bay's largely barren salt flat alongside imagery from 2017, by which point thousands of acres had filled in with the reed, which can reach 10 to 15 feet tall. The dense stands block sheet flow across the lakebed and trap sediment that raises ground elevation, keeping water from reaching the lake, though the exact volume lost is not known. Hambrecht argued the reed can be controlled effectively and that replacing it with native species, while slow and difficult, is worth the effort.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Australia's Firmus to launch $5 billion IPO on October 6, term sheet shows
item.description: Australian data centre operator Firmus will launch its initial public offering on Oct. 6, seeking A$7 billion (about $5 billion) in what would be the second-largest IPO in the country's history, according to a term sheet reviewed by Reuters. The institutional bookbuild runs Oct. 6 to 7, a prospectus is expected Oct. 8, retail bidding opens Oct. 12 through 19, and shares are due to begin trading on the Australian Securities Exchange on Oct. 22. With an over-allotment option the company could raise up to $5.5 billion, adding an extra $500 million — a greenshoe structure common internationally but used unevenly on the ASX. Founded in 2019 by Oliver Curtis, Tim Rosenfield and Jonathan Levee, Firmus would rank as the fourth-largest IPO globally this year on Dealogic data. An investor presentation indicates the founders' shares will be held under escrow after listing; the company declined to comment.
item.dc:creator: Christine Chen and Scott Murdoch, Reuters

item.title: SoftBank launches $11 billion bonds to fund OpenAI investment
item.description: A term sheet seen Monday shows SoftBank Group has launched a sale of $10 billion and €1 billion in senior unsecured notes to finance its investment in OpenAI. The dollar tranche is split across 3.5-, 5.5- and 7.5-year maturities and the euro tranche across four- and six-year maturities. At the planned size it would be the largest non-financial corporate bond deal on record for Asia Pacific and Japan, topping 7-Eleven's $10.93 billion sale in January 2021 according to LSEG data, and would rank among the 20 biggest globally this year per Dealogic. Proceeds are earmarked for SoftBank's $10 billion payment on the third tranche of its follow-on OpenAI investment, expected to close Oct. 1, and will cancel an earlier $10 billion bridge loan. Pricing is set for Sept. 24 with settlement Sept. 29; SoftBank declined to comment on the term sheet.
item.dc:creator: Kane Wu and Yantoultra Ngui, Reuters

item.title: Audit recommends changes after examining Salt Lake City Public Utilities' $600M debt
item.description: A report released Tuesday by the Office of the Legislative Auditor General found no evidence that Salt Lake City misused enterprise funds, but concluded the city's Department of Public Utilities took on more than $600 million in debt with no workable plan to repay it. The debt is tied to a new water reclamation facility and the City Creek water treatment plant, projects that together cost over $1 billion and which department officials say federal standards required. Auditors said the resulting short-term fixes drove steep sewer rate increases for non-residential customers, including an estimated increase of more than 110% for schools, charities and churches after the department changed its sewer rate model in fiscal year 2025. They also said the department could not demonstrate the new charges were accurate, equitable or consistently applied. Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, said the findings raise big questions and urged the department to look for ways to cut costs.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL
