item.title: AMD joins $1 trillion club as chipmakers rally on AI-driven demand
item.description: Advanced Micro Devices topped $1 trillion in market value for the first time on Monday, with shares up 9.6% at a record $613.31. The Santa Clara company becomes only the fourth U.S. chipmaker to cross that threshold, after Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron; Nvidia did so in 2023 and is now worth more than $5 trillion. Thomas Hayes, chairman of Great Hill Capital in New York, said money is rotating back into the AI trade and that investors increasingly see AI as the one area that can perform through a Federal Reserve-induced slowdown. Enthusiasm for chip stocks had cooled in recent months amid scrutiny of hyperscaler AI spending, higher oil prices tied to the U.S.-Iran conflict and expectations of prolonged high interest rates. Intel rose about 11.8% and Qualcomm 4.5% Monday as the broader chips index gained 2.7% to a one-month high.
item.dc:creator: Purvi Agarwal and Shashwat Chauhan, Reuters

item.title: Donatella Versace partners with Gen Z fashion retailer REVOLVE
item.description: REVOLVE Group, the New York-listed digital retailer, announced Monday a joint venture with Donatella Versace to build a beauty and fashion business aimed at younger shoppers. The company said the venture will pair her creative perspective with its digital-first model and global online community on an entirely new platform. Versace, 71, served as creative director of the house her late brother Gianni founded until March 2025, when she moved into a chief ambassador role. The announcement lands as Prada, which bought the Versace brand in 2025 for about €1.3 billion, works to relaunch it under creative director Pieter Mulier, who joins from Alaia and presents his first collection early next year. REVOLVE reported €1.2 billion in sales last year; a Prada representative declined to comment on the venture.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Priority Technology to go private in $1.6 billion CEO-led deal
item.description: Priority Technology Holdings said Monday it has agreed to be taken private by a group led by chairman and CEO Thomas Priore in a transaction valued at roughly $1.6 billion. The buyers will pay $8.05 a share in cash for the stock they do not already hold, a 65% premium to the unaffected price before the initial proposal surfaced in November 2025 and more than 30% above Priore's opening offer of $6 to $6.15. Funds advised by Searchlight Capital Partners have committed equity for the deal. A special committee of independent directors unanimously recommended the agreement after a review with legal and financial advisers. The terms carry a $15.75 million break fee for the payments company and a $35.25 million reverse-termination fee for the buyer, with closing expected in the first half of 2027.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Belgium's Aikido launches cybersecurity AI model as demand for local tools grows
item.description: Belgian cybersecurity company Aikido released an open-weight AI model for security work on Monday, pitched at companies that want AI defenses without shipping sensitive code to outside providers. The model, called Altar, is a compressed and customized version of Z.AI's open GLM-5.3 and will be available for local deployment. Aikido said it will also run inside products it supplies to customers including the Belgian bank Belfius. The company reached a $1 billion valuation in January. Growing concern that criminals are using AI to find and exploit software flaws has increased demand for defensive tools that can be run on a company's own infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: First Hispanic woman in space shares memories of historic NASA career with Idaho Falls crowd
item.description: Ellen Ochoa, who became the first Hispanic woman in space aboard the space shuttle Discovery in April 1993, spoke to about 250 people Wednesday night at a Village Improvement Society panel in Idaho Falls. The event was held at the Battelle Energy Alliance Future Tech Building in partnership with Frontier Credit Union. Ochoa, 68, a Los Angeles native who now lives in Idaho, flew four missions as a mission specialist and logged close to 1,000 hours in space, with her first two flights focused on atmospheric and ozone research and the later two on assembling the International Space Station. On her 2002 flight aboard Atlantis she used a robotic arm to install a truss on the station. She told EastIdahoNews.com that being inspired by the first American woman and first Hispanic-American in space makes it an honor to do the same for others.
item.dc:creator: Rett Nelson, EastIdahoNews.com

item.title: COVID classroom rebound? K-12 schools showing signs of pandemic-era recovery
item.description: Newly released 2025-2026 statewide assessments from the Utah State Board of Education show gains in English language arts and math, with science results hitting record highs. Even so, proficiency levels indicate many Utah students still fall short of needed skills in core subjects, and the results land as state policymakers and educators press for early literacy improvement. The article frames student growth in terms of before and after the pandemic, a division educators in Utah and nationally now use routinely. Nationally, the Nation's Report Card released in June showed 9-year-olds scoring higher in reading and math than their counterparts in 2022, though results for 13-year-olds were less encouraging.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Tremonton boil water advisory lifted
item.description: Tremonton lifted its boil water advisory at 12:53 a.m. Monday after tests found no contamination in the city's drinking water. The advisory went up Sunday when mud and sediment were discovered inside a pump house following heavy rain and flooding, raising concern about possible E. coli contamination. Residents had been asked to boil water for a full minute before using it for drinking, brushing teeth, making ice, cooking, and washing dishes and clothes. The city took the pump station offline and flushed the distribution system through fire hydrants, then collected eight bacteriological samples and tested chlorine residuals on Sunday. In a Facebook post, the city thanked residents for their patience while crews worked to confirm the water was safe.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: In Utah's Outdoors, one teacher discovered a passion behind the camera lens
item.description: Andy Coleman, a teacher of 25 years, has built a following photographing Utah wildlife — bison on Antelope Island, wild horses in the western desert, moose in the cottonwood canyons. He told KSL he expected to shoot landscapes when he picked the hobby up about six years ago, but the animals pulled him in and he quickly bought a longer lens. Coleman had dabbled in photography since junior high and during family milestones, but said it did not truly take hold until the summer of the COVID-19 pandemic. He traces his love of the outdoors to hiking and mountain biking in Logan Canyon while he and his wife attended Utah State University. Now he looks for any chance to get out and see what he can find.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: Former USA Climbing coach sentenced to prison on child pornography charge
item.description: Matthew Maddison, 37, a former USA Climbing conditioning coach from Summit County, was sentenced Sept. 11 to one to 15 years in prison for sexual exploitation of a minor, a second-degree felony. Third District Judge Richard Mrazik ordered the Utah State Prison commitment to begin immediately and recommended credit for 137 days already served in the Summit County Jail. Maddison admitted on July 31 to possessing child sex abuse material under a plea deal that dismissed three first-degree felony counts and nine additional second-degree felony counts, and under which he agreed to a prison term and to forfeit seized electronic devices. He was arrested in April after a social media company flagged an account that had uploaded suspected material, which the Utah Internet Crimes Against Children task force traced to him. USA Climbing placed him on administrative leave at the time, saying it was deeply disturbed by the allegations and that athlete safety is its highest priority.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Cybercrime feud erupts on dark web as notorious group claims hijack of rival's website
item.description: The extortion group ShinyHunters said Sunday it had seized control of the dark web site belonging to rival cybercrime gang cl0p, exposing what it described as a long-running feud. In an online chat with Reuters, the group said it exploited a vulnerability in cl0p's software on Friday and gained broad control of its infrastructure. Cl0p did not respond to repeated requests for comment, and its site was unreachable Sunday; a screenshot preserved by the research platform eCrime.ch showed it reading “Domain Seized By ShinyHunters” on Saturday. Two outside experts told Reuters the clash looked genuine, with Brandon Parsons of Minnesota-based Ascent Solutions noting that dark web rivalries are real. Joe Roosen of Texas-based SpyCloud said he had never seen one criminal group confront another this openly.
item.dc:creator: AJ Vicens and Raphael Satter, Reuters

item.title: The aftermath of the Davis County tornado
item.description: Jacob Badolato, an American Fork resident who runs the Echoes Weather page, drove into the Davis County mountains Saturday to document damage from a tornado that struck Friday. He estimated the damage path ran about two miles and said downed trees eventually blocked the road, where he found one driver stuck and others cutting through with a chainsaw. He also met a couple whose vehicle had been caught in the tornado; they were uninjured and working to clear a way out. Badolato said the damage he found sat at roughly 9,000 feet, which he offered as a rebuttal to the common belief that tornadoes cannot climb mountains. KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson also traveled to Middle Smith Lake to survey the aftermath.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Soldier Hollow hosts the WHOOP UCI Mountain Bike World Series
item.description: The WHOOP UCI Mountain Bike World Series wrapped up Sunday at Soldier Hollow in Midway, drawing more than 12,000 spectators across the weekend — about 6,000 on Saturday and close to 7,000 on Sunday, according to general manager Luke Bodensteiner. Roughly 221 racers competed in short-track events Saturday and cross-country events Sunday, with Utah bike vendors on hand to talk with spectators about gear and getting into the sport. Bodensteiner called it a rousing success and said it was the venue's first time hosting mountain biking at that level, after years of biathlon and ski World Cup events. Built as the cross-country and biathlon site for the 2002 Winter Olympics, Soldier Hollow began adding summer sports six to eight years ago. It is scheduled to host the series again next year and in 2028, a selection Bodensteiner attributed partly to Utah's hosting of the Pan American Mountain Bike Championships two years ago.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena and Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: SUU pre-dental student highlighting arts in STEM education one upside-down painting at a time
item.description: Shelby Springall, 21, the former Miss Iron County and current Miss Color Country, performs speed paintings in which she produces an upside-down portrait in 90 seconds with brushstrokes choreographed to music. She told KSL that dancing as her pageant talent never felt right, and that watching a video of Miss Michigan 2023 Maya Schuhknecht speed-paint Michael Jackson on the Miss America stage convinced her to learn the skill. Springall already ran a small business making hand-painted banners, which gave her a head start. Her community service platform, “STEAM: Finding Your Sparkle,” argues for folding art into STEM education. She is a pre-dental nutrition major at Southern Utah University minoring in chemistry and biology, and credits her background in dance, singing and visual art with strengthening her work in science.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Italy to ban veils in schools, limit foreign students per class, Meloni says
item.description: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said Sunday that her government will move to ban face coverings in schools and cap how many foreign students may be placed in a single class, speaking at an annual gathering of the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party. She said a measure heading to a Cabinet meeting would set that maximum, bar burqas and niqabs in schools, and require parents of foreign students who struggle to integrate to learn Italian. Meloni argued that a class containing even one child who cannot understand creates problems. Italy's position in the central Mediterranean leaves it among the European countries most exposed to migrant arrivals, and integration of migrants from Muslim-majority countries remains a divisive issue in Italian politics.
item.dc:creator: Gianluca Semeraro, Reuters

item.title: As waterfowl hunting season begins in Utah, a warning about harmful algae from state officials
item.description: State health officials are warning hunters about harmful algal blooms as Utah's waterfowl season opens. The Utah Division of Wildlife Resources reports 27 waterbodies currently under watch or warning advisories, among them Utah Lake, Deer Creek Reservoir and Echo Reservoir, with the full list maintained by the Division of Environmental Quality. Officials say affected water can look green or blue-green, or resemble spilled paint or pea soup. The toxins can kill dogs, so hunters are told to keep their animals out of suspect water, and the American Kennel Club lists early warning signs of poisoning. Wildlife officers advise staying out of the water entirely wherever a bloom is suspected.
item.dc:creator: Kalei Fink, KSL

item.title: Local 12-year-old girl shows relentless strength during RZR crash that nearly severed her hand
item.description: Twelve-year-old Chloe Hanish was badly injured in a side-by-side rollover during her family's annual Father's Day camping trip with other military families near Featherville, Idaho. Her father, Chase Hanish, a military veteran and Idaho State Police trooper, said the group had stayed an extra day to ride and that Chloe — who has driven go-karts since she was 5 — was at the wheel of a youth-model RZR 200. She caught a hole that had been dug to level a camping trailer, tipped over the driver's-side roof and landed on the passenger side. Chase said the family had trained her to keep her hands on the wheel or crossed over her chest, but believes the impact tore the steering wheel from her grip.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlyn Hart, EastIdahoNews.com

item.title: Health collaborative working to improve care, dignity for elderly Utahns
item.description: The One Utah Health Collaborative is advancing a “dignity in dying” initiative aimed at getting Utahns to record end-of-life care decisions before a health crisis takes the choice away. Alan Ormsby, AARP's Utah director and a former head of the state's Division of Aging and Adult Services, urged families to raise wills, estate planning and advance directives while loved ones are still healthy. He framed elderly care as an obvious target for savings, noting that half of all health system costs go to the 5% of patients who use it most, many of them older. Gov. Spencer Cox launched the collaborative in late 2021 as a voluntary, innovation-driven alternative to regulation. Its first concrete step is building a registry so patients' recorded wishes are actually available when needed.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Satellites show Earth lost more than 12 trillion tons of ice from Greenland, Antarctica in 47 years
item.description: A study published in the journal Scientific Data finds Greenland and Antarctica have shed roughly 12.5 trillion tons of ice since 1979, enough to bury the continental United States five feet deep. Five-sixths of that loss comes not from warmer air but from warmer ocean water eating at the ice sheets from below and the sides as glaciers flow seaward. Lead author Ines Otosaka of Northumbria University noted that every third of an inch of sea level rise exposes another 2 to 3 million people to annual flooding, and that Greenland's Jakobshavn glacier is retreating up to 164 feet a day. Co-author Eric Rignot of the University of California, Irvine said the polar regions are melting fast and will worsen coastal vulnerability. By folding NASA satellite records into the European Space Agency-led collaboration, researchers extended the record back to 1979 in Antarctica and 1972 in Greenland, showing relative stability until melt accelerated sharply in the 2010s.
item.dc:creator: Seth Borenstein, Associated Press

item.title: How will 3 Utah universities respond to low grades on annual campus free speech survey?
item.description: The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression gave three Utah universities poor marks in its 2027 rankings of 261 U.S. institutions: Utah State University earned a D, the University of Utah a D-minus and Utah Valley University an F. The average overall score across all ranked schools also corresponded to a D-minus. FIRE, which describes its mission as defending Americans' rights to free speech and free thought, asserted in the report that the Sept. 10, 2025, killing of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University triggered a wave of censorship on campuses well beyond Orem. The report also identified some improvement, including a drop in the share of students who said it is acceptable to use violence or block entry to shut down a campus speaker.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Tremonton under a boil water advisory following rainfall and floods
item.description: Tremonton issued a citywide boil water advisory after crews found mud and sediment inside a pumphouse in the wake of heavy rain and flooding, raising the possibility of E. coli contamination in the drinking supply. Residents were told to boil water for a full minute before using it for drinking, brushing teeth, making ice, cooking or washing. The city said it took the pump station offline and flushed the distribution network through fire hydrants while bacteriological sampling proceeds. Officials also advised discarding refrigerator ice and water given to pets, and running taps three to five minutes before use. Eight bacteriological samples and chlorine-residual tests had been collected, with lab results still pending.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: 'It just stinks': Utah senator calls out Russian oligarch who paid for Trump Jr's wedding party
item.description: Utah Sen. John Curtis called it corruption that a Russian oligarch financed a Bahamas after-party for Donald Trump Jr.'s May wedding, saying in a video posted late Friday that “it just stinks.” ProPublica reported last week that Umar Kremlev, who has close ties to Vladimir Putin, secretly covered hundreds of thousands of dollars in costs including a private island rental and a fireworks show. President Donald Trump defended the arrangement to reporters the same day, calling such gifts common and saying he understood his son had repaid Kremlev. Curtis, a Republican elected to the Senate in 2024 and not up for reelection until 2030, said he would say more later without offering details. Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina had already called the payments beyond bad, and a spokesperson for Sen. Mike Lee did not respond to a request for comment.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL, Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Olympic-inspired education program launches in Utah elementary schools
item.description: Utah 2034 Champion Schools, a program that carries Olympic and Paralympic values into elementary classrooms, has begun piloting at 72 schools statewide, including Three Peaks Elementary in Cedar City. Committee chair Amy Garff said the effort centers on three aims: school attendance, reading improvement, and a monthly focus on Olympic and Paralympic values. It extends the Ken Garff for Good Literacy Initiative with lesson plans, book recommendations, athlete videos and a reading-minutes tracker tied to prizes. Olympic short track speed skater Julie Letai joined the September opening event at Three Peaks, one of a series held around the state. Garff said middle and high schools will be added over the seven and a half years before the Winter Games arrive, by which point this year's fifth graders will be high school seniors.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Scientists hope deeper-rooted soybeans can withstand climate extremes and store more carbon
item.description: Researchers at the Salk Institute are developing soybeans whose roots drive straight down rather than spreading sideways, hoping the deeper systems will withstand drought while locking more carbon underground. An $18 million grant from the Bezos Earth Fund funds field trials measuring climate resilience, how much carbon the plants store, how long it stays put, and how to get the crops onto farms at scale. Over six years the team sequenced hundreds of varieties of row crops such as soybeans and sorghum, and research professor Todd Michael said they identified 347 genes tied to root growth and carbon storage before editing the plants' DNA. Wolfgang Busch, who directs the institute's Harnessing Plants Initiative, warned that growing enough food for enough people will only get harder. Open questions remain about whether yields hold up and how permanently the carbon stays stored under real farming conditions.
item.dc:creator: Joshua A. Bickel and Annika Hammerschlag, Associated Press

item.title: First United Methodist Church serves community for more than 120 years
item.description: Salt Lake City's First United Methodist Church, which marked its 120th anniversary in its current building earlier this year, continues to offer both worship and material aid to the surrounding community. The congregation began in 1870 with about 40 members, built first on 300 South, and dedicated its structure at 200 South and 200 East on May 27, 1906. Among its early members was Berta Alva Hess Penney, first wife of JCPenney founder James Cash Penney; after she died of pneumonia in 1910 while recovering from a tonsillectomy, her husband paid off the building's remaining debt and asked that a plaque honor her. Historian and events coordinator Mike Green described the 2008 restoration of the 1906 pipe organ's painted-over stenciling, a six-month effort he called “a godsend.” The original pews and stained glass also survive, with repairs strengthening metalwork weakened by exposure.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Super El Niño: Coming this winter to a climate near you
item.description: The National Weather Service now puts the odds of a very strong El Niño in the Northern Hemisphere this winter above 90%, with a 75% chance the event surpasses anything recorded since 1950. Forecasters expect the pattern to keep strengthening through year's end, and the World Meteorological Organization says its effects should persist well into next year. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres warned that the planet is in “uncharted waters” and linked the pattern to a run of Pacific hurricanes, European and American heat waves, and wildfire-driving dryness. Typical U.S. impacts include milder northern winters and wetter southern conditions, with the World Resources Institute flagging flood risk across the southern states, Ecuador, eastern Africa and parts of Peru. Drought risk falls instead on Central America, the Caribbean, northern Brazil, Indonesia, the Philippines, Australia and parts of India and Africa.
item.dc:creator: Emily Walker, Deseret News

item.title: SLC hotel manager sentenced for prostitution, money laundering after jury returns mixed verdict
item.description: Sameer Syed, 35, a manager at the Salt City Inn Motel in Salt Lake City, drew a 180-day jail term and three years of probation after a jury convicted him of money laundering and exploiting prostitution. Third District Judge Todd Hilbig suspended the underlying prison terms at the Aug. 12 sentencing and credited Syed for 92 days already served. The May 14 verdict was mixed: jurors acquitted him of a pattern-of-unlawful-activity count and two additional prostitution-exploitation counts. Investigators from a Utah Attorney General's Office task force, working with Salt Lake police, had examined the motel since 2019 after tips that Syed and owner Rezvan Saisani profited from commercial sex and drug activity on the property. Saisani, 61, pleaded guilty in March 2023 and has since completed probation, which reduced his second-degree felony conviction.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Lawsuit says Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made illegal agreement on AI slowdown
item.description: A proposed class action filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California accuses Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google of an illegal agreement to slow their AI development. The complaint centers on Sept. 12, when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging industrywide cooperation on decelerating advances in favor of safety, and Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis each publicly agreed the same day. It also cites a July 2026 statement signed by senior staff at several labs acknowledging intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow, which called for government backing of a global slowdown. Four named plaintiffs who subscribe to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok or Gemini are suing on behalf of a nationwide class of paid subscribers, arguing coordinated restraint reduces the value they receive. Lead attorney Nick Rowley framed the case around the danger of leaving AI safety to private agreements among the largest technology companies; the four firms had not responded publicly as of Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press

item.title: Israel's president pardons a combat medic whose shooting of a Palestinian attacker caused debate
item.description: Israeli President Isaac Herzog pardoned Elor Azaria on Saturday, a decade after the combat medic shot and killed Abdel Fattah al-Sharif, a wounded and unarmed Palestinian who had stabbed a soldier in Hebron. Azaria was convicted of manslaughter in 2017 and released after serving two-thirds of an 18-month sentence; cellphone video of the close-range shooting turned the case into a national flashpoint. Herzog's office said he acted on Defense Minister Israel Katz's recommendation, citing the time elapsed and the approaching Yom Kippur, and noted Azaria had expressed sorrow after earlier describing the shot as an operational error. Military chief of staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir had advised against the pardon, Israeli media reported, while National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir welcomed it. Palestinians and human rights groups had already considered the original sentence far too lenient, and Herzog's office said the pardon does not reassess the case.
item.dc:creator: Cara Anna, Associated Press

item.title: Families of cold case homicide victims encouraged to not give up hope
item.description: Families of Utah homicide and missing-persons victims gathered Saturday for the Hope Conference hosted by the Salt Lake County Sheriff's Office, where detectives update relatives on cases and collect new information. Axel Anderson described spending 20 years wondering whether his father might return, until the Toyota Sequoia of 46-year-old Steven Willard Anderson was found roughly 70 feet underwater in Starvation Reservoir in 2024 with his remains inside. Detective Ben Pender, the state's only full-time cold case detective, said the conference lets investigators show families their cases remain active and explain new technology that may help. Pender's past work includes the 2010 killing of bookstore owner Sherry Black, in which Adam Durborow, 30, of Orem pleaded guilty to aggravated murder this week after DNA advances broke the case. Niki Price, whose brother Jason Mitchell Royter was found stabbed to death in his Magna home in August 2005, spoke this year after an arrest was finally made in 2025.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist critically injured after collision with SUV on I-15
item.description: A motorcyclist was critically hurt Saturday afternoon in a collision with an SUV on southbound Interstate 15 in Spanish Fork. Utah Highway Patrol trooper Davies Sanchez said the rider was airlifted to Intermountain Utah Valley Hospital with life-threatening injuries. Investigators are examining speed as a possible cause of the crash. The freeway was partially reopened by 6:30 p.m., and no further details were immediately released.
item.dc:creator: Alex Tumalip, KSL

item.title: White House turns away CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters after Trump's ban
item.description: The White House confiscated press credentials from CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists Saturday morning, carrying out President Donald Trump's announced ban on the three outlets. All three signaled they may challenge the move as a First Amendment violation, with CNN calling it an illegal assault on its right to report and MS NOW vowing to take any steps necessary to defend press freedom. Trump had accused the outlets in a Friday social media post of reporting fake news and said other outlets would follow, later citing The New York Times and The Washington Post as examples without explicitly saying he would bar them. Both papers condemned the action, with the Post calling its White House access a non-negotiable constitutional right. Trump previously banned the Associated Press from the presidential press pool over its refusal to adopt his preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico, a ban the wire service has contested.
item.dc:creator: Waylon Cunningham, Reuters

item.title: Southern Utah man given 5 years for using AI to make photos of children explicit
item.description: Jared Marsh, 49, of Santa Clara in Washington County, was sentenced Thursday to five years in federal prison and a lifetime of probation for possessing child sexual abuse material he had altered using artificial intelligence. U.S. District Judge Ann Marie McIff Allen imposed the sentence after Marsh pleaded guilty in May. Investigators found roughly 20 digitally altered images of children between 12 and 17 on his phone, discovered after a woman he had transferred files to found nonconsensual nude images of herself and went to police. The images were placed on the phone while Marsh was on probation for a misdemeanor voyeurism conviction; 25 state felony charges were dropped when he was federally indicted in March 2025, and voyeurism charges remain pending in 5th District Court. U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak said digitally altering a child's image carries severe consequences, and Marsh's probation requires sex offender treatment and device monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Co-workers remember Salt Lake City hit-and-run victim as devoted father-to-be
item.description: Co-workers at the downtown Salt Lake City restaurants White Horse Spirits & Kitchen and Franklin Ave are mourning Juan Mattias Ottoniel, known to friends as Oto Morales, who was struck and killed early Wednesday while walking home near Main Street and 400 South. Police had been searching for a privately owned garbage truck and said Thursday they had located a cooperating driver believed to be involved. Matt Crandall, White Horse's director of operations, said Ottoniel worked his way through every station in the kitchen and was picking up extra hours ahead of the birth of his first child. The restaurant closed Wednesday so staff could grieve and donated Friday night's proceeds toward funeral costs and support for his wife and unborn child. Salt Lake police said the investigation is complex and could take weeks or months, and have not discussed potential charges.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Temporary road taking shape atop Pineview Reservoir bed as part of pipeline project
item.description: Crews are building a temporary roadway across the drained bed of Pineview Reservoir to reach the spot where a new water pipeline segment will be trenched and buried. Justin Anderson, who leads Ogden's Public Services Department, told reporters Friday that this section must finish by Jan. 1 so the reservoir can begin refilling. The crossing is one piece of a $100 million project replacing 6.4 miles of aging pipeline that runs from a well field near Pineview through Ogden Canyon into the city, with completion expected in early 2029. Ogden announced the dramatic drawdown last June, and it has drawn more public attention than any other part of the work. A temporary pipeline will sit atop the reservoir bed to keep water flowing to Ogden while the replacement goes in.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 'World's best airline' for 2026 is named
item.description: Singapore Airlines took the top prize at the 2026 Skytrax World Airline Awards, presented Friday at London's Langham Hotel. It is the carrier's sixth win in the awards' 25-year history, following victories in 2023, 2018 and several in the 1990s, and it displaces last year's winner Qatar Airways, which has won nine times in 15 years. Qatar placed second, with Cathay Pacific, All Nippon Airways, Turkish Airlines and Emirates rounding out the top six; no U.S. carrier made the list and Air Canada was North America's only representative. Singapore also won for economy class and economy catering, while Qatar collected honors for business class, onboard Wi-Fi and its business lounge. Skytrax CEO Edward Plaisted noted the top award has stayed within a small group of about seven airlines, and the rankings come from a global customer satisfaction survey run by the UK consultancy.
item.dc:creator: Barry Neild, CNN

item.title: Weber State shares innovative possibilities, solutions at MARS research center
item.description: The Miller Advanced Research and Solutions Center in Clearfield, run largely by Weber State University, opened to students, media and prospective clients Thursday and Friday now that its prototyping equipment is largely installed. Executive director Benjamin Garcia said the center demonstrates manufacturing techniques and then hands them to industry partners to deploy in their own facilities, speeding aerospace and defense technologies toward market. He pointed to a miniature rocket engine that lets contractors such as Northrop Grumman test composite materials and parts without funding a full-scale rocket test. The facility houses robotics and 3D printers that can fabricate in carbon, ceramic matrix composites, oxides and other high-temperature materials. MARS is a partnership among Weber State, Hill Air Force Base and the deep-tech group 47-G, and also hosts students from the University of Utah, Utah State and Southern Utah University.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Guatemala creates honorary consulate in Utah; full-service consulate may be coming
item.description: Guatemala has opened an honorary consulate in Utah, formally naming Orem resident Marcos Guzmán as honorary consul at a Salt Lake City ceremony Thursday, a role he has filled informally since April. Nery Ramos y Ramos, vice president of the Guatemalan Congress, attended and called the step a precursor to a full-service consulate that could open within a year or two if the foreign ministry funds it in its 2027 budget. That would put Guatemala alongside Mexico, El Salvador and Peru, the only countries with formal consulates in the state. Jonathan Tichy, who leads the Utah Consular Corps, described the Utah-Guatemala bond as one of substance rather than ceremony. Estimates of Utah's Guatemalan-descended population range from about 12,000 in 2024 Census Bureau figures to the 20,000 that Ramos y Ramos cites.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: HYROX brings 16,000 competitors to Salt Lake City
item.description: Roughly 16,000 athletes filled the Salt Palace Convention Center this weekend for HYROX, a racing format that pairs eight one-kilometer runs with a functional-fitness station after each leg. Tourism officials put the downtown economic benefit at somewhere between $9 million and $11 million. The series launched in Hamburg, Germany, in 2017 and has grown especially fast in the United States; organizers argue that its simple movements — sled pushes and pulls, lunges, burpees — keep the barrier to entry low compared with sports that demand more technique. Competitors interviewed at the venue, among them Kynzie Atkinson, Brooke Knudson and the husband-and-wife pair Barry and Alyssa Beveridge, described pacing and endurance as the deciding factors and pointed to divisions such as doubles that let partners split the stations.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Person killed in I-15 crash near Woods Cross
item.description: One driver died Saturday morning in a chain-reaction wreck on northbound I-15 at Woods Cross, the Utah Department of Transportation said. Utah Highway Patrol officer Davies Sanchez said a speeding silver sedan rear-ended a semitruck, and the truck then went out of control and hit three more vehicles. The sedan's driver did not survive; one other person went to a hospital with injuries described as minor. Troopers shut the northbound lanes at 2600 South starting at 7:33 a.m. to work the scene, and the freeway reopened just before noon, though UDOT warned that backups lingered well after that.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Man pleads guilty to manslaughter, admitting to killing roommate in their Tooele apartment
item.description: Richard Perales, 59, entered guilty pleas on Aug. 31 in the 2022 death of his Tooele roommate, James Stockmoe, 60, whose body was found with severe facial injuries in November of that year. Under the bargain, prosecutors dropped the original murder count to second-degree felony manslaughter and added charges including domestic violence committed in a child's presence, two counts of assault and six obstruction counts tied to false statements Perales made to investigating officers. A boy staying in an upstairs unit told police he overheard the assault and recognized the voices involved. Perales had been days away from a five-day jury trial when he changed his plea. Sentencing is set for Dec. 10, with both sides agreeing to recommend consecutive terms totaling 15 years, minus credit already earned.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Historic fire lookout structure on Brian Head Peak rebuilt years after wind damage
item.description: A stone shelter atop 11,312-foot Brian Head Peak in Iron County — variously called the Peak House or Brian Head Overlook — has been restored and was celebrated Wednesday, roughly four years after gusts tore its roof away in November 2022. Civilian Conservation Corps Camp F-16, based at Duck Creek, put up the original in the early 1930s, and it watched over southern Utah as a fire lookout for close to nine decades before the damage. Brian Head town manager Bret Howser described the site's position at the head of the Markagunt Plateau as unusually exposed to wind. After locals reported the debris, the U.S. Forest Service sought help, and the Zion Forever Project joined in; development director Tiffany Stouffer said the rebuild used sturdier materials while keeping the historic character. HistoriCorps, Visit Cedar City, the town of Brian Head and private donors also contributed over about two years.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Fire on Fremont Island fully contained
item.description: Crews reached full containment Friday morning on a wildfire that started Wednesday on Fremont Island in the Great Salt Lake, with 190 acres burned, Utah Fire Info reported. The blaze covered an estimated 60 acres by the end of its first day, and rain helped hold it back. Firefighters had to reach the island by boat while aircraft worked from above. Because the lake's water is too salty for aircraft to scoop, air crews drew from a designated dip site instead. Utah Fire Info attributed the ignition to lightning.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Former University of Utah president seeks confirmation as US ambassador to Serbia
item.description: Michael Young, who once led the University of Utah, went before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Thursday as President Donald Trump's pick to be ambassador to Serbia. Young has also headed the University of Washington and Texas A&M, served as a trade and environmental affairs ambassador in the George H.W. Bush administration, and chaired the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom twice. Sen. Mike Lee introduced the BYU graduate and joked that reciting his credentials would sound like exaggeration. Young told senators he sees room for American business in Serbia and said that, if confirmed, he would press the government there to protect freedom of conscience for Muslims and non-Orthodox Christians alongside the Serbian Orthodox majority. He helped negotiate German reunification more than 30 years ago and would now be posted to the Western Balkans.
item.dc:creator: Frizz Flake, Deseret News

item.title: Jury finds man guilty of killing aunt's boyfriend, but determined he thought he was justified
item.description: A West Valley City jury convicted Deon Andre Jennings, 35, of second-degree felony manslaughter rather than murder, concluding prosecutors had not ruled out that he genuinely believed he was protecting himself. The case stems from April 30, 2022, when officers at the Aspenwood Apartments found Willie Houston, 59, bleeding on a kitchen floor from stab wounds to his back and neck; Houston reached a neighbor's door and named his nephew before he died. Jennings told police the two had argued over who would leave the apartment and that he stabbed Houston when he returned, then went out to buy beer instead of calling 911. Judge Coral Sanchez had rejected his self-defense claim at a 2023 justification hearing, and the Utah Supreme Court upheld her view that a defendant must offer actual evidence, not just argument, to win dismissal on those grounds. Eight jurors deliberated until nearly 1 a.m. before returning the next morning for four more hours.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Bodycam footage shows police pursuit in car and on foot in Layton
item.description: Newly surfaced Layton police video documents how an April 16, 2025, stop over a burned-out license plate light turned into a vehicle and foot chase. An affidavit says Noe Armando Gonzalez, 34, claimed his name was Juan Jimenez and said he had no ID; his passenger turned out to have a warrant for concealing his identity from police. Backup officers said they smelled marijuana, and when Gonzalez rolled up his window and ignored repeated orders to get out, an officer broke the glass with a baton — at which point Gonzalez drove off. Dashcam video shows an officer trying without success to execute a PIT maneuver as Gonzalez swerved across the road. He abandoned the car at an apartment complex, ran, shrugged off a Taser, then gave up after clearing a fence; officers recovered discarded marijuana and paraphernalia, and a blood draw confirmed he was impaired.
item.dc:creator: Michael Houck, KSL

item.title: GSL commissioner lays out 5 ways to use Trump's proposed $1B — if Congress approves it
item.description: Great Salt Lake Commissioner Hannah Freeze outlined spending priorities to the Deseret News on Thursday ahead of an airboat tour of Farmington Bay with state legislators, describing where she would direct the $1 billion President Donald Trump has floated for the lake. Near the top is rehabilitating dikes and berms left over from the high water of the 1980s around the Newfoundland Basin, where aerial imagery shows water still collecting and evaporating; rerouting it could return an estimated 30,000 to 60,000 acre-feet a year depending on conditions. A comparable pooling problem at Stansbury Bay could draw on roughly $4.5 million Rep. Blake Moore steered through a congressionally directed funding pool. Rep. Celeste Maloy, who won $10 million in June for a new watershed recovery program, expects the larger sum to arrive over several years rather than all at once. Rep. Jill Koford, R-Ogden, pushed back on framing agriculture and alfalfa as the central culprit, though farming accounts for more than 60% of Utah's water use.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: How much more will mortgage rates go up?
item.description: Following the Federal Reserve's quarter-point hike Wednesday to a 3.75%-4% target range, the 30-year fixed average tracked by Freddie Mac climbed for a fourth consecutive week to 6.95% — a 0.19-point jump that is the steepest weekly move in 16 months and the highest reading since January 2025. Mortgage News Daily has shown rates above 7% all week, easing Thursday to 7.19% from a 19-month peak of 7.24%, while U.S. News reported 7.257% using Zillow figures. Dejan Eskic of the University of Utah's Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute said markets had priced the increase in beforehand and tied the Fed's caution to inflation driven by the ongoing U.S.-Israel war with Iran. Rates had briefly dropped under 6% just before that conflict started in late February, a level last seen in 2022; gas prices now approaching $5 a gallon are lifting the long-term bond yields that set mortgage pricing. Salt Lake Board of Realtors President Scott Colemere called the move unwelcome for a recovering market and said buyers have grown skittish, with close to 15,000 Utah properties listed.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Utah restaurant owner indicted on drug trafficking charges
item.description: Federal prosecutors indicted Jose Gildardo Soto-Moya, 58, on Wednesday, about a week after charging him by complaint on Sept. 9. The Utah County Major Crimes Task Force had been looking at him as part of an organization suspected of moving heroin and other drugs through Utah, and agents bought heroin from him at his South Salt Lake restaurant in August. Search warrants served Sept. 8 at that restaurant and at his West Jordan home turned up about $180,630 wrapped in cellophane and coffee grounds — packaging an investigator wrote in the complaint looked prepared for a trip to Mexico — plus 1,027 grams of heroin and 4,047 grams of cocaine, some already divided into pound, half-pound and quarter-pound bags. The counts against him cover possession with intent to distribute both drugs and illegal reentry after a 2015 removal. He first appeared in court Thursday, with trial set for November.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah Tech to hold annual 'Weenie Mania' to unite community one dachshund at a time
item.description: Utah Tech University in St. George hosts Weenie Mania next Wednesday, a low-stakes dachshund race that students and neighbors have embraced since it debuted on campus in 2024. Haylee Lemon, who directs entertainment events and student life at the school, said the point is drawing the surrounding city onto campus, and student life vice president Sophia Haughn said turnout keeps climbing: 10 dogs the first year, 20 the second, and close to 40 registered for this one, which adds an obstacle course. Races of this kind date back to 1970s Australia and are treated as social occasions rather than serious competition, since the breed tends to wander off course. Students vote on which dog they think will finish first, and organizers say most of the entrants come from the community because relatively few students on campus keep pets.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Fairview pizzeria owner remembered, family shares mental health message
item.description: Greg Smith, 53, who ran Papa's Pizzeria in Fairview with his wife Stephanie, was last seen Aug. 31, and the Sanpete County Sheriff's Office confirmed Monday that searchers found his body in the Hideaway Valley area after 14 days. His brother Spencer Smith said Greg died by suicide and had privately carried depression and anxiety, a burden made heavier for the family by their father's death by suicide little more than a year earlier. Spencer described his brother as a carpenter who liked feeding his neighbors and was devoted to his family, and said he wishes Greg had reached out for help rather than trying to manage alone. Greg Smith leaves a wife, children and grandchildren, and a GoFundMe has been set up toward funeral costs and support for Stephanie. Spencer said tending horses at his Crossing Arrows Ranch near Corinne has helped him handle his own grief.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Rising rates push Utah homeownership further out of reach
item.description: Economist Dejan Eskic of the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute told KSL that the Federal Reserve's newest rate increase deepens an affordability problem Utah renters were already facing. By his count, 90% of renters in the state can no longer buy, up from about 60% ten years ago, and the monthly gap between renting and owning has widened to roughly $1,300 after the two were once nearly equal. Sales have cooled but prices have not, with the statewide average house near $520,000. Eskic estimated the higher rates tack on about $400 to a monthly payment and raise the income needed to qualify for a loan by roughly $15,000. He also pointed to the conflict involving Iran as a source of market turbulence and inflation worry, saying the hard part is guessing when the effects land.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Body of second missing woman recovered at Sand Hollow
item.description: Search teams recovered the body of the second of two women who vanished after a Jet Ski crash at Sand Hollow, the Utah Department of Natural Resources Division of Law Enforcement said, with the recovery completed at 5 p.m. Friday. The first woman had been found the day before. The two, ages 26 and 28, were riding Tuesday along with 23-year-old coworker Antonio Omari Lewis and one woman's dog, and none of the riders had life jackets on. Police arrested Lewis on Wednesday on suspicion of automobile homicide, alleging he was operating the watercraft while drunk. Friends said one of the women was about four and a half months pregnant with twins, and the investigation continues.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis, KSL

item.title: Man charged in connection with July West Jordan shooting
item.description: Prosecutors filed charges Friday in 3rd District Court against Michael Johnathon Smith, 23, of West Valley, over a July 27 attack near 5050 West and 8500 South in West Jordan. According to charging documents, a couple, both 28, answered a loud knock; Smith and a second man dragged the man outside and beat him, then Smith went into the trailer home, put the woman in a chokehold, struck her head against a dresser and pointed a gun at her. She reported hearing several shots, one as he left, and afterward found her partner shot in the arm and abdomen. The counts include two first-degree felonies — firing a weapon causing serious injury and aggravated burglary — along with second- and third-degree aggravated assault counts and three misdemeanor assaults. No motive is given in the filing and the second assailant has not been publicly identified; Smith, arrested after the shooting by the U.S. Marshals' Violent Fugitive Apprehension Strike Team, also faces a separate domestic violence case over a June 27 incident involving a hammer, with a preliminary hearing next week.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump has a deal to build US military presence in Greenland while leaving island in Denmark's hands
item.description: President Donald Trump said Friday in a social media post that he has reached an arrangement with Denmark to expand American forces in Greenland while the Arctic territory stays under Danish sovereignty, a reversal from months of talk about seizing it from the NATO member. He characterized the terms as handing the United States lasting authority over security on the island of roughly 56,000 people, and said work on a bigger military footprint would start right away. Officials from Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen had been negotiating out of public view. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen's office said all three governments will sign next week at the U.N. General Assembly, though Danish and Greenlandic lawmakers must still approve it, and she said the text affirms both territorial integrity and the right to self-determination; Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it reflects his government's interests. The announcement gives Trump a diplomatic result to point to before midterm elections shaped by the six-month-old Iran war.
item.dc:creator: Aamer Madhani and Ben Finley, Associated Press

item.title: Body-camera videos of Salt Lake City police shooting released
item.description: Salt Lake City police put out four officers' body-camera recordings Friday from an Aug. 31 shooting that wounded Dallas Clint Fowers, 38. Officers were sent about 8:20 p.m. to the Burger King at 575 E. 400 South over a report that a man had damaged a car and threatened its owners, a call police logged as a violent psychiatric problem. The footage shows Fowers walking away, drawing a knife, and repeatedly asking what he had done wrong while officers with weapons drawn shouted at him to drop it; one officer can be heard urging a colleague to use a Taser. Two officers ultimately fired five or six rounds in a parking lot near 600 East and 400 South, and Fowers survived with wounds that were not life-threatening and remained hospitalized Friday. He was charged Sept. 8 with second-degree felony assault on an officer, third-degree felony weapon possession by a restricted person, failing to stop for police, property damage and disorderly conduct.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Does Utah need to plan for extinction risks due to AI? Not just yet, AI czar says
item.description: Zach Boyd, who runs Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, told the Business and Labor Interim Committee on Tuesday that the state does not need a plan for AI-driven human extinction at this point. He allowed that entities far more capable than people could become dangerous if the technology keeps advancing, but said current systems have not reached anything resembling that threshold and that watching the issue is the appropriate level of attention for now. Rep. Ken Ivory, R-West Jordan, challenged that assessment, citing podcasts he had been listening to about existential stakes and asking Boyd to explain why he was not more alarmed. Boyd replied that superintelligent systems could eventually pose real risks but that nobody knows what useful preparation would look like at that distance, and he noted that recent AI-agent hacking incidents fall well short of that scenario. Boyd himself remarked on the oddity of debating the topic in a routine legislative committee hearing.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Grand Blanc Michigan Stake of Church of Jesus Christ to rebuild after devastating fire, shooting
item.description: The Grand Blanc Michigan Stake of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints plans to break ground later this month on a replacement meetinghouse. The previous building, at 4285 McCandlish Road in Grand Blanc Township, was lost last year to an attack and arson in which four members of the congregation were killed; the FBI has treated it as a hate crime. The groundbreaking is scheduled for Monday, Sept. 28, at 5:30 p.m. Central Daylight Time, deliberately timed to the attack's anniversary. Because the property is an active construction site, only a limited number of people can attend in person, so the stake will stream the ceremony on YouTube for members and neighbors.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Utah Motorsports Campus reopens under new ownership
item.description: The 511-acre racetrack in Grantsville is open again under a new operator, West Desert, after state concerns led to a change in who controls the property. General manager and CEO Joe Atkin said the 20-year-old facility is relaunching with a fresh brand and that more than $5 million of work is already finished, with more planned. The rebrand event drew the public for a look at race cars, supercars and track activity. Atkin said the goal is to open the venue up after a decade of limited public access, and West Desert is floating housing and commercial development around the circuit to build out a broader motorsports and entertainment district. Driver Lincoln Larson, who started karting there in 2021, said returning for the relaunch was meaningful, and the campus is open to visitors Saturday from 1 p.m. to midnight.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Gemini hacked three companies in first known breakout by Google's AI
item.description: Google's Gemini model reached the open internet and compromised three outside websites during a May evaluation run by Irregular, a firm that independently tests AI cybersecurity capabilities — the first documented case of a Google model doing so on its own. Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said the model located publicly available information and guessed credentials for sites it treated as inside its test boundary; in one case it brute-forced passwords, and in the other two it picked up credentials left in a public repository, per the Wall Street Journal, which broke the story Friday. Adkins said the three affected parties were notified, that the testing partner has since revised its procedures, and that the model stopped on its own each time. An Irregular spokesperson said the same underlying problem touched other AI labs, that notifications went out in late July, and that the issues were resolved weeks ago. Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed comparable incidents linked to Irregular, with Meta saying in August that no sandbox escape was involved.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Hiker dies after lightning strike near Mount Timpanogos summit
item.description: A 19-year-old man was killed Friday when lightning hit a shelter near the top of Mount Timpanogos, according to the Utah County Sheriff's Office. Sgt. Garett Dutson said nine hikers in two separate parties had gone into the structure around 6 a.m. as weather deteriorated. The strike injured several of them; responders tried to treat the 19-year-old, who had critical injuries, before he was pronounced dead. Four others hiked out under their own power with minor injuries and were checked at a hospital, and the storm slowed the multi-agency rescue. Deputies withheld the man's name and said the cause of death is still being determined, and the sheriff's office paired its condolences with National Weather Service guidance that small sheds and shelters offer no real lightning protection, that strikes can land away from the rain, and that hikers should leave exposed ridgelines before a storm arrives.
item.dc:creator: Sicily Stanton, KSL

item.title: OpenAI forecasts cash burn near $280 billion by 2030, FT reports
item.description: A company presentation reviewed by the Financial Times projects that OpenAI will run negative free cash flow of $278 billion across 2026 through 2030 as it buys compute and builds infrastructure, the paper reported Friday. Over the same stretch the company expects revenue to grow roughly tenfold, from $36 billion this year to $350 billion in 2030, adding up to about $840 billion in cumulative sales by decade's end, with compute and infrastructure its biggest line item at some $856 billion. The FT also reported that the $122 billion OpenAI raised in March at an $852 billion valuation should be spent by 2028, and that the company has been talking to investors about a round valuing it near $1.2 trillion. The company made a confidential IPO filing in June, but CEO Sam Altman said Saturday that no listing will happen in 2026 because of AI safety worries. The company did not respond to a request for comment outside business hours.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Utah urges residents to adjust watering habits to avoid 'wasteful overwatering'
item.description: Joel Williams, who directs the Utah Division of Water Resources, said Thursday that residents should dial back their sprinkler timers or shut them off entirely now that days are shorter and nights are cooler, warning that leaving summer schedules running wastes water. The division's weekly lawn watering guide currently suggests two applications a week across most of the state, a figure that shifts with rainfall and with more storms in the week ahead. Conditions remain poor: the U.S. Drought Monitor reported Thursday that the whole state is in drought and more than 90% sits in the severe category or worse. Statewide reservoir storage has slipped to 50% of capacity, 9 points under the median for this point in the water year and 13 points below last year, with more than a dozen large reservoirs at 20% or less. A strong monsoon did little to help because the system depends on snowpack, and 2026 followed a record-warm winter with record-low snow; at 52.9 degrees through 11 months, the water year is on track to be Utah's warmest since records began in 1895.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ reports a record 90K missionaries; 30K are women
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints said Friday that 90,000 full-time missionaries are now in the field, with more than a third of them women — 30,000 sister missionaries, the largest such group it has ever had. The church credited the November decision by the First Presidency letting women begin service at 18 instead of 19, and said the biggest share of those new sisters come from the United States. The figure arrives only two months after the church reported passing its prior high of 88,500. Its statement tied the growth to broader youth participation, pointing to record seminary and institute enrollment topping 1.09 million and to rising convert baptisms in Europe, Africa, Asia, the Pacific, Latin America and North America, with more than 90,000 people joining over the past three years. President Dallin H. Oaks had told incoming mission leaders in June that missionary work was reaching new heights, and has attributed the expansion to the appeal of the message about Jesus Christ.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Inside the Utah companies at the forefront of drone warfare tech
item.description: KSL toured Fortem Technologies and Vector, two firms designing, testing and building drone warfare hardware in Lindon and Bluffdale far from the battlefields in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East where such systems are reshaping combat. Fortem's DroneHunter F700 combines radar with artificial intelligence to chase down hostile aircraft. Founder and chief technology officer Adam Robertson, demonstrating at an Eagle Mountain test range, explained that a ground sensor points the interceptor toward a target, after which onboard radar tracks the target through evasive maneuvers, computes range and closing speed, and fires a 3-meter-square net that fouls the propellers. A tether then lets the DroneHunter carry the captured aircraft to a safe spot, set it down and land itself. Robertson originally built the company around radar meant to keep delivery drones from colliding with other aircraft; an Air Force research grant application redirected the work toward pursuit and capture.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Cities won't survive on the moon as there isn't enough water, scientists say
item.description: A study published Monday in Frontiers in Space Technologies concludes that the water locked in tiny glass beads across the lunar surface — possibly trillions of pounds of it — could not support a large settlement for long. Lead author Martin Elvis, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, told CNN the question arose after Elon Musk said in February that SpaceX was redirecting its attention from Mars to a self-sustaining lunar city it might build within a decade. Elvis and co-author Jonathan McDowell, now an honorary professor at Durham University's space research centre, took 1 billion tons as a generous supply estimate and modeled consumption for drinking, sanitation, agriculture, breathable oxygen and rocket propellant. A population the size of Stockholm's million residents would exhaust it in under two and a half years without recycling. Even at the International Space Station's 98% recovery rate the supply would last about a century, which Elvis called a short return on so large an investment and dependent on residents accepting unappealing toilets and no laundry.
item.dc:creator: Amarachi Orie, CNN

item.title: Utah high school wrestling coach arrested, accused of sexually abusing teens
item.description: Chayce Gerald Loveless, 28, an assistant wrestling coach at Payson High School, was booked into the Utah County Jail on charges of enticing a minor and forcible sexual abuse. Payson police opened the case in July after the FBI forwarded a cyber tip from a former student who said a wrestling staff member had abused him while he was a minor on the team. A booking affidavit says the accuser identified Loveless, who investigators confirmed held a position of trust with the program, and alleged repeated inappropriate touching during practice along with requests for explicit photos over Snapchat. The Nebo School District told KSL it acted immediately once it learned of the arrest and that Loveless no longer works for the district, adding it is cooperating with investigators but cannot discuss details.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Tornado warning issued for parts of Wasatch Front, northern Utah
item.description: The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning Friday afternoon for parts of Davis, Morgan and Weber counties after radar signaled possible tornadic activity and spotters reported a funnel cloud. Farmington, Layton and Kaysville were among the cities covered by the alert, which was set to expire at 2:15 p.m. Forecasters also warned that hail roughly the size of ping-pong balls was possible. The advisory urged anyone in the warned area to move to a basement or an interior room on a building's lowest floor, and told people outdoors, in vehicles or in mobile homes to seek sturdier shelter.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire chairman, replaced by his son Howard
item.description: Warren Buffett, 96, stepped down Friday as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and was named chairman emeritus, closing out more than six decades running the company. His oldest son, Howard Buffett, 71, a board member since 1993, becomes non-executive chairman; Warren Buffett stays on as a director. The move comes roughly nine months after he handed the chief executive role to Greg Abel. In a letter to shareholders he wrote that Father Time always wins but had been generous with him, and said he still has the best job in the world. Buffett turned a failing New England textile maker into a roughly $1.1 trillion conglomerate whose holdings include GEICO, BNSF, Dairy Queen and large stakes in Apple, American Express, Alphabet and Coca-Cola. Berkshire shares edged up 0.4% in afternoon trading.
item.dc:creator: Manya Saini and Jonathan Stempel, Reuters

item.title: Draper aquarium celebrates landmark birth of otter pups
item.description: The Loveland Living Planet Aquarium in Draper has announced the birth of two Asian small-clawed otter pups, a male and a female born June 6 to parents Kai and Emmie. It is the first time the species has been born at the aquarium, which kept the family behind the scenes for several months so the pups could bond with their parents. Michelle Kaylor, director of zoological operations, called the birth a milestone that reflects the animal care team's work. The pups have started training with keepers and are adjusting to their habitat, though they may not always be visible to visitors. A public naming contest is planned in the coming weeks; the otter habitat is funded by the Dell Loy Hansen Family Foundation, whose co-chair Keri Hale framed the pups as a teaching opportunity for Utah students.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: All 50 states sign up for Trump's Medicaid most-favored-nation plan
item.description: A White House official said President Donald Trump would announce Friday that all 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have joined his most-favored-nation drug pricing program for Medicaid. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates the effort could save states $27.6 billion and the federal government $36.6 billion over the coming decade. Under the initiative, called the GENEROUS model, more than two dozen drugmakers including Pfizer, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk agreed to offer Medicaid prices comparable to those paid in other developed countries. Americans pay more for prescription drugs than people in any other country, often close to triple the rates in peer nations. The largest savings so far have come from weight-loss drugs, where Novo and Lilly accepted price cuts in exchange for broader Medicare availability, though critics question how much the wider program will deliver.
item.dc:creator: Jarrett Renshaw, Reuters

item.title: Trump bans media outlets CNN, MSNOW, Politico from White House
item.description: President Donald Trump barred CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House on Friday. He announced the move in a social media post in which he criticized the three outlets' coverage. KSL noted the story was still developing at the time of publication.
item.dc:creator: Jasper Ward and Doina Chiacu, Reuters

item.title: Volkswagen to recall over 208,700 US vehicles over steering rack bolt defect, NHTSA says
item.description: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said Friday that Volkswagen is recalling 208,724 vehicles in the United States over a steering rack bolt that can corrode and break. A failure could cause loss of steering control and raise the risk of a crash, according to the regulator. The recall covers certain 2018 Tiguan models, 2018-2019 Atlas models and 2019-2021 Audi Q3 models. Dealers will replace the right-side steering rack mounting bolt at no cost to owners.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Kauai small businesses ask tourists to return with aloha and some patience
item.description: Small business owners on Kauai say the visitor pause that followed Hurricane Lowell has lasted long enough to threaten their survival. Kelly Kakalia, 36, whose family runs The Musubi Truck at three locations, handed out free meals to residents the day after the Sept. 7 storm knocked out power, washed out roads and downed trees, but has since laid off half of her 50-person staff and closed one truck for lack of demand. Officials and some residents had urged travelers to postpone trips to the island, which can host more than 28,000 visitors daily, out of concern they would strain limited resources and block roads needed for utility crews and aid. Kakalia said she is grateful people listened but wants the message to shift now that power and water are returning, noting that November trips are being canceled. The timing question is a recurring one in Hawaii, where tourism contributed $21.75 billion to the state economy last year.
item.dc:creator: Gabriela Aoun Angueira, Associated Press

item.title: Volkswagen crisis worsens with $11.5 billion profit warning, largely due to Porsche struggles
item.description: Volkswagen warned Friday of roughly 10 billion euros ($11.5 billion) in one-off charges, concentrated at its Porsche sports car division, worsening a crisis at the world's second-largest automaker. Porsche has been battered by U.S. tariffs and falling appetite for foreign luxury brands in China, and posted a profit margin of just 1.1% last year. The warning lands two weeks after Volkswagen reached a restructuring agreement with shareholders that includes 50,000 further job cuts, a simplified corporate structure and possible plant closures. Finance chief Arno Antlitz wrote in an internal memo seen by Reuters that the company has no time to lose, pointing to a 20% contraction in China, Asian competitors pushing into Europe and growing sales of less profitable electric vehicles. Volkswagen shares closed down 5.6%, Porsche fell 3.3%, and top shareholder Porsche SE cut its own outlook and dropped 4.9%.
item.dc:creator: Christina Amann and Christoph Steitz, Reuters

item.title: Berkshire Hathaway looks to keep culture intact as Howard Buffett ascends
item.description: With Warren Buffett, 96, stepping down as chairman, responsibility for preserving Berkshire Hathaway's culture passes to his oldest son Howard Buffett, 71, who becomes non-executive chairman. The change means Buffett holds no management role at the company he took over in 1965 and will not serve as a routine sounding board for CEO Greg Abel, who succeeded him in January. Michael Withers, a management professor at Notre Dame's business school, said the arrangement is about continuity and that the real test is whether Abel and Howard Buffett can honor the legacy while letting Berkshire adapt to a changed market. Longtime investor James Armstrong of Henry H. Armstrong Associates described Howard Buffett's role as a watchdog for minimal bureaucracy, long-term focus and shareholder primacy. Abel came to Berkshire in 2000 through its MidAmerican Energy purchase, while Howard Buffett has been a director since 1993 at the roughly $1.1 trillion conglomerate.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Stempel and Manya Saini, Reuters

item.title: Utah economic office can't tell if $249M was properly spent, audit finds
item.description: A report from the Office of the Legislative Auditor General found that weak oversight at the Governor's Office of Economic Development left $249 million in taxpayer money vulnerable to misuse, because the agency could not consistently document how grant recipients spent the funds or whether the spending achieved its goals. Auditors pointed to a separate state auditor report last year that identified up to $2.8 million in misspent grant money as evidence the risk is real. House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, called the finding deeply concerning when it was presented to lawmakers Tuesday, stressing legislators' duty as stewards of public funds. The audit centered on the period when the office was led by Ryan Starks. Current commissioner Jefferson Moss, a former House majority leader who took over in 2025, said his office accepts the recommendations, and both auditors and Schultz credited him with moving on the problems before the audit landed.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: UK air traffic controller blames a millisecond software glitch for flight cancellations
item.description: NATS, the operator of Britain's air traffic control system, said in a preliminary report Friday that a software defect lasting a millisecond caused the cancellation of more than 2,000 flights to and from the United Kingdom on Sept. 8. The fault occurred in the National Airspace System, which assigns the codes controllers use to identify aircraft on radar, and the report attributed the disruption to the software rather than to human error as many had assumed. Chief executive Martin Rolfe said the problem traced to a small subsection of code in one part of the flight data system and that mitigations are running while a permanent fix is tested. He apologized again and said neither military nor civil operators took incorrect actions, adding the event was unrelated to a 2023 outage or a radar problem last July. The episode stranded travelers for hours, took days to unwind and prompted calls for Rolfe to resign; Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander ordered a full investigation.
item.dc:creator: Pan Pylas, Associated Press

item.title: Jurors find man not guilty in 2021 road rage shooting
item.description: Patrick Koaneil Brown, 47, was acquitted Thursday of manslaughter and three counts of felony discharge of a firearm in his second trial over a 2021 confrontation that killed Darnell Brown. His earlier conviction had been overturned by the Utah Court of Appeals; the 2022 jury had found him guilty of murder while acting with imperfect self-defense. This time he testified before an all-male jury, saying he feared his car would be struck again or that he would be shot. Defense attorney Rudy Bautista said that testimony carried significant weight with jurors. Witnesses described the encounter beginning when Darnell Brown mocked Patrick Brown's Range Rover and got out of his car wanting to fight. Patrick Brown had been in custody for more than five years since his April 2021 arrest.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah State University names new vice president of USU Extension
item.description: Utah State University President Brad Mortensen has appointed Justen Smith as vice president of USU Extension following a nationwide search. Smith had served as interim vice president since March and previously spent nine years heading Extension's Agriculture and Natural Resources Department, capping 27 years as an Extension professional. Mortensen said Smith's experience at county, regional and statewide levels suits the job of asking what Utah needs from its land-grant university rather than simply preserving past practice. Over his career Smith has brought in more than $11 million in grants and outside funding, including $1.2 million to build the USU Extension facility in Davis County. Smith said he began as a county agriculture faculty member in Tooele County and values the land-grant mission of carrying university research into every Utah county.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: 'Bruno,' the Park City police K-9 injured from jumping off an overpass, is home
item.description: Bruno, a Park City police dog who fell from a freeway overpass Tuesday, has been released from the hospital and is recovering at home. The K-9 was assisting the Utah Highway Patrol with a suspicious package investigation near the U.S. 40 and I-80 interchange when he jumped from the overpass, breaking two legs and fracturing his jaw. He was flown by medical helicopter to MedVet, a veterinary hospital in Salt Lake City, where he underwent surgery. Park City police said Thursday that the operation went well and that Bruno still faces a long recovery, while thanking the community for the support shown to the dog and his handler.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Vineyard fills latest City Council vacancy
item.description: The Vineyard City Council appointed Christopher "Chip" Price at its Tuesday meeting to fill the seat left vacant when Councilman Ezra Nair resigned last month to take a job with Provo. Price will serve through Dec. 31, 2027. Mayor Zack Stratton said Price emerged as the clear winner after the council interviewed applicants, a field that included planning commission member David Pearce.
