Price, who has worked in IT for two decades at Ascent Programs, a group operating homes for troubled youth, told the council that skills in listening, de-escalation and finding middle ground would help him address divisions in the city. He said he wants to pursue creative solutions as Vineyard grows, clean up waste left by redevelopment sites, and broaden the tax base to ease what he called residents' taxation fatigue.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah mom-to-be finds support through group prenatal care
item.description: Elizabeth Snow, a first-time mother, educator and boxing coach, is going through her pregnancy alongside other women due around the same time through CenteringPregnancy, a group prenatal care model. Jennifer Rolley, a nurse midwife with Intermountain Health, said the approach rests on three parts: health assessment, interactive learning and community support. Two-hour group sessions replace many conventional prenatal visits while preserving individual care, with participants recording their own weight and blood pressure and meeting one-on-one with a midwife before the group discussion. Those discussions range from bodily changes during pregnancy to labor, delivery and adjusting to a newborn, and groups can decide whether partners attend. According to the Centering Healthcare Institute, the model is in use at hundreds of sites across more than 40 states and territories.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: ICE officer pleads not guilty to charges he lied to the FBI about nonfatal Minneapolis shooting
item.description: Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro, 52, pleaded not guilty Friday before a U.S. magistrate judge to six federal counts of making false statements about a Jan. 14 shooting in Minneapolis. Prosecutors say Castro fired through the front door of a home, wounding 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg, then told investigators he had been attacked with a broom handle and a snow shovel beforehand. Minnesota charged him in May but struggled for months to extradite him from Texas, where he had been arrested; after officials warned he might cross into Mexico upon release from a Texas jail, he surrendered to federal authorities following his separate federal indictment this month. The federal appearance came a day after he faced state assault charges and was released from custody. Defense attorney Daniel Gerdts declined to comment. It is the Justice Department's first prosecution of a federal officer over conduct during this year's immigration crackdown.
item.dc:creator: Tim Sullivan, Associated Press

item.title: Idaho man handed 6 years in prison for assaulting southern Utah park rangers
item.description: Gregory Aaron Farley, 52, of Hazelton, Idaho, was sentenced Thursday to more than six years in prison for driving his pickup into two U.S. Park Rangers in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. Rangers had stopped Farley in May 2025 after a report of reckless driving, and charging documents say he fled, nearly striking one ranger, then drove erratically during the pursuit before turning around and hitting the rangers' truck on the driver's side hard enough to deploy its airbags. Rangers fired at the vehicle, and Farley surrendered after a prolonged standoff, receiving treatment for a gunshot wound to his left thigh. He pleaded guilty in December to assaulting federal employees with his truck. Prosecutors had sought seven years, citing 10 prior DUI convictions, two of them felonies that sent him to state prison.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Police announce resolution to 2005 West Valley cold case homicide
item.description: West Valley City police said Thursday they have resolved the 2005 killing of Sheree Allen, naming her then-boyfriend Carl Swanigan, who died in 2013, as the primary suspect. Det. John Wells told KSL that investigators had enough evidence and probable cause to reach that conclusion, and that three separate reviews of the case file backed the department's finding. Allen's body was found in a dumpster on Jan. 24, 2005, by a man searching for valuables. Wells said Swanigan had been a prime suspect early on because he was the last person known to be with Allen and DNA evidence connected him to her, and that investigators believe domestic violence played a role. Allen's mother, Lillie Allen, said she felt grateful and joyful that a long journey had finally closed.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Costco, Uber expanding delivery to more states
item.description: Costco and Uber have struck a partnership that widens Uber Eats delivery of Costco goods from 17 states to 47. The arrangement covers nearly 600 warehouse locations, and Uber says the full range of Costco items will be orderable through the app. Shoppers will need to verify their Costco membership before placing an order. CNBC reported that the deal could grow Uber Eats' customer base while exposing younger shoppers to Costco's bulk-buying membership model.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Charges filed in ongoing dispute with neighbor that culminated with shooting
item.description: Burkeley Jerald Priest, 53, was charged Thursday in 7th District Court with aggravated assault resulting in serious injury and discharging a firearm causing serious injury, both second-degree felonies, after a Sunday shooting at cabins near Scofield Reservoir in Carbon County. Police responded around 3:30 a.m. to a reported burglary and shooting; the wounded man, shot in the upper thigh, was flown by medical helicopter to a hospital. According to a booking affidavit, the victim made it to a bathtub in the cabin where he was staying, and officers found a large amount of blood there. A man who had brought his family to the cabin for the weekend told police he drove the victim toward the road to reach cell service and met an officer who applied a tourniquet. Witnesses described a long-running property dispute between the neighbors, with that man saying Priest routinely carried a gun and had threatened to shoot him about a year earlier for walking on his property.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'Seeing is believing': Utah senators tour Great Salt Lake as they look at ways to protect it
item.description: Several Republican state senators spent about an hour Thursday morning touring Farmington Bay by airboat with newly confirmed Great Salt Lake Commissioner Hannah Freeze as they weigh future legislation on the lake. Freeze told lawmakers that despite a weak snowpack last winter, the lake should avoid the record low it hit in 2022 and currently sits roughly a foot above that mark of 4,188.5 feet, which she attributed to recent conservation and legislative work even though levels remain unhealthy. Senate Majority Whip Chris Wilson, R-North Logan, on the lake for the first time, was splashed with mud when his airboat stopped abruptly but said the trip left him struck by the birds overhead. Wilson called the lake a continuing high priority and said the modest gain still leaves substantial work ahead. Utah Department of Natural Resources employees piloted the boats, and John Luft of the Division of Wildlife Resources noted the lake draws close to 12 million birds each year.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Chinese 'robot brain' startup sees ChatGPT-style breakthrough as soon as next year
item.description: Gao Yang, co-founder and chief scientist of Beijing-based Spirit AI, told Reuters at the company's offices Thursday that humanoid robots should be able to carry out most general-purpose tasks from spoken instructions as early as next year, though household usefulness remains further off. He called the brain the weakest link in the robotics stack, reflecting an industry shift from hardware feats like sprinting and backflips toward the software behind embodied AI. Gao said he expects a GPT-3.0-equivalent milestone by mid-2027, at which point a person could speak to a robot in natural language and get a reasonable sequence of physical actions. Spirit AI employs roughly 1,000 contractors across China who wear sensor equipment at home or in factories to capture how people move, and a visit to its Beijing training center showed workers repeating actions such as opening refrigerators, unlocking safes and cutting vegetables. The company's robots currently succeed at about 90% of simple tasks in structured living-room settings.
item.dc:creator: Laurie Chen, Reuters

item.title: Weber County sales tax taking effect Oct. 1 expected to generate $13.1M a year
item.description: A 0.2 percentage point sales tax increase that Weber County commissioners approved in June takes effect Oct. 1 and is projected to raise about $13.1 million annually, much of it for transportation and public safety. The change lifts the rate in most county cities from 7.25% to 7.45%, an effective 2.8% increase in what shoppers pay; Riverdale moves from 7.45% to 7.65% and Huntsville from 8.25% to 8.45%. County officials said little about the specifics when they approved it, but an informational document from the Wasatch Front Regional Council provided to KSL breaks down the projected revenue by locality, including $127,934 earmarked for unincorporated areas. Commissioner Gage Froer had promoted the tax, permitted under state law, as a way to raise revenue without increasing property taxes. Davis County commissioners approved a comparable increase Tuesday, though theirs does not begin until Jan. 1.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Police cancel missing and endangered advisory for baby boy
item.description: The Utah Department of Public Safety has canceled a missing and endangered advisory for an infant boy it had asked the public to help locate Thursday. Officials said at the time they believed the child was with his mother and her boyfriend, who is the boy's father. The department initially described the child as one year old and later corrected his age to nine months.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Family works to restore monument for former apostle, Salt Lake City mayor
item.description: Descendants of Daniel H. Wells are raising $10,000 to restore the granite monument that has marked his grave at the Salt Lake City Cemetery for at least 125 years, after cemetery staff asked whether the family wanted to take on the project. Great-grandson Quentin Wells, 84, said monuments cost as much to restore as to install, and the money would cover cleaning the stone, adding new plaques and returning it to its original condition. Daniel H. Wells came to Utah with Latter-day Saint pioneers in 1848, served as superintendent of public works for the church, and in 1857 became an apostle and a counselor to church President Brigham Young. He also spent 10 years as mayor of Salt Lake City, led military forces in Nauvoo and Utah, and served as territorial attorney general before statehood. Quentin Wells, who published a biography of his great-grandfather with Utah State University Press in 2016, described him as a major influence across roughly 40 years who remains surprisingly little known.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Lindsey Vonn warns fans about scammers impersonating her online
item.description: Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn posted on Instagram warning that fake accounts are impersonating her, her family members and people she works with, and that some are soliciting money or personal information from fans. She told followers that any account claiming to be her and asking for money, donations or personal details is not her. The warning tracks a pattern KSL Investigators documented earlier this year, in which scammers use fabricated social media profiles, artificial intelligence and deepfake tools to pose as athletes and celebrities. That technology can produce convincing images, video and voices, making impersonation harder to spot. The earlier Get Gephardt investigation found con artists borrowing Olympians' identities to build rapport with fans before asking for money.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt, KSL

item.title: Utah politicians differ on future of power plants after Trump administration repeals emission rules
item.description: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin completed the rollback of Biden-era power plant emissions rules on Sept. 14, an action the agency says will spare the industry $310 billion, and immediately proposed eliminating the remaining greenhouse gas standards for another $370 billion in claimed savings. The repeal removes most of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, with the EPA arguing the rules demanded control technologies that were not adequately proven and effectively pushed plants toward closure rather than setting attainable targets. Utah House Public Utilities and Energy Committee Chair Colin W. Jack, R-St. George, an electrical engineer and former Dixie Power executive, called the old rule a direct threat to modern life and said he is relieved it is gone, noting the change touches only carbon dioxide and leaves limits on particulates, sulfur, mercury and nitrogen oxides intact. Sen. Nate Blouin, D-Salt Lake City, countered that he expects about 1,000 additional deaths a year and argued that tighter emissions rules also reduce asthma, cancer and other illness. Blouin added that regulating carbon dioxide alone still has knock-on effects for other pollutants.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Preserving Salt Lake Temple was 'nothing short of another miracle,' project official says
item.description: Georges Bonnet, communications director for the Salt Lake Temple and Temple Square renovation, told a full auditorium at the University of Utah on Wednesday that the seven-year effort to seismically secure the temple rivals the miracle of its original 40-year construction. Speaking as part of the university's William R. and Erlyn J. Gould Distinguished Lecture on Technology and the Quality of Life, he spent more than an hour on the retrofitting work and on what temples mean to members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The temple opened in 1893, long before research into the Wasatch Fault released in the 1970s prompted Wasatch Front builders to design for earthquakes, and the church announced structural and seismic work in 2019. Bonnet avoided the word renovation, describing the project instead as a renewal meant to extend the building's legacy far into the future. Construction began in 2019, and scaffolding came down earlier this year as remaining work moved indoors.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: A rare look inside: Carmelite Monastery opens grounds for annual fair
item.description: The Carmel of the Immaculate Heart of Mary Convent in Holladay opens its grounds to the public once a year for the Carmelite Fair, a fundraiser supporting cloistered nuns who otherwise rarely leave the monastery. Life there is ordinarily given over to silence, prayer and contemplation. Sister MaryAnn of the Ascension Krajicek, 98, a discalced Carmelite who has served the Catholic Diocese of Salt Lake City for more than 68 years, said the community keeps silence all day not for its own sake but to hear the Lord interiorly. Originally from Nebraska, she entered religious life at 30 and was assigned to the Holladay monastery, and said she prays most for the people of Utah because that is where she was sent. She described the life as simple by design and said the nuns are there to love and praise God.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Police identify man hit, killed by truck in Salt Lake City
item.description: Salt Lake City police have identified Juan Mattias Ottoniel, 20, as the man killed when a truck struck him and fled early Wednesday in downtown Salt Lake City. Officers happened to be on an unrelated call nearby and found him within minutes of the collision near 15 West and 400 South, performing lifesaving measures until medics took him to a hospital, where he died. Witnesses reported that Ottoniel was in the crosswalk when he was hit and was dragged some distance by the vehicle. Investigators initially sought a privately owned garbage truck thought to be involved, and by Thursday the department said it had located both the vehicle and a cooperating driver.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: September declared 'Utah's Own Month' to honor local agriculture
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox has designated September as Utah's Own Month, a new annual observance recognizing products grown and made in the state. The designation is meant to honor Utah farmers, ranchers, food producers and local businesses while encouraging residents to buy from them. September was selected because it covers harvest season, when locally grown food is at its peak. Officials noted the recognition carries extra weight this year because Utah producers have contended with drought, freezes and fires. Utah's Own plans markets, events and promotions across the state through the month.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Trump withdraws Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, as his nominee to lead ICE
item.description: The White House said Thursday it is withdrawing the nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper with little immigration experience, to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The withdrawal leaves an agency central to President Donald Trump's domestic agenda without a Senate-confirmed director for longer still, and the White House offered no explanation in its brief statement. Schroyer is close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former Oklahoma senator who took over the department in March. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, had declined to hold a confirmation hearing until DHS provided information he requested about civilian deaths during ICE enforcement operations, telling the Associated Press his objection was not to the nominee himself. The agency has faced intense scrutiny over how it recruited and trained officers while hiring thousands to carry out mass deportations, including shootings that killed multiple people such as two American citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Health Secretary Kennedy adds 8 new members to key health committee
item.description: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. appointed eight new members Thursday to the Preventive Services Task Force, the 16-member panel that determines which preventive medical services must be covered for patients at no cost. The task force normally meets three times a year but last convened a year ago, after its November meeting was canceled by a 2025 government shutdown and an earlier July meeting was abruptly called off by the health department. Kennedy removed the panel's chair and vice chair in May, and a Supreme Court ruling last June affirmed his authority over the committee. He has similarly reshaped other federal health advisory bodies, including dismissing and replacing the entire membership of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee last year. The new appointees include pediatric hematologist-oncologist Seth Corey, pediatrician Patrick Hunter, cardiovascular expert Ronald Karlsberg, health finance specialist Stephen Parente, preventive cardiology professor Venkatesh Murthy, family medicine physician Goldie Stands-Over-Bull and gastroenterologist Louis Wilson; HHS declined to say when the panel will next meet.
item.dc:creator: Sriparna Roy, Reuters

item.title: Judge orders Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major changes
item.description: U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center on Thursday to give 30 days' notice before making major physical changes to the building, including demolition, which President Donald Trump has threatened. Cooper said the ruling was meant to avoid confusion after recent events, including the center's abrupt closure to the public on Wednesday. Executive director and chief operating officer Matt Floca said he closed the performing arts center temporarily because of acute public safety risks from continued structural deterioration, with at least a seven-day shutdown to assess severely deteriorated portions of the main building and a possible extension after next week's evaluation. Floca said the temporary closure is separate from the board's Tuesday vote to close the center indefinitely for repairs, which followed an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier in the month. The ruling came in a case brought by Ohio Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, a trustee who sought an emergency hearing over what she called an unlawful closing.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Daly, Associated Press

item.title: New Salt Lake City housing opens for people leaving homelessness
item.description: KWB Apartments, a new five-story supportive housing complex at 44 N. 1000 West in Salt Lake City, has opened with 67 permanent apartments for people leaving long-term homelessness who also live with serious mental health conditions. The $26 million project, funded through a mix of public and private sources, is a partnership between First Step House and Housing Connect, and offers on-site mental health care, case management and recovery support. First Step House CEO Shawn McMillen said the building is meant to be a lifelong housing option rather than transitional shelter, citing data that the large majority of residents in this model stay housed indefinitely. Program manager Erik Enriquez described helping residents move from a difficult environment into a welcoming home as deeply inspiring.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Lost evidence should result in dismissal of Douglas Carter's death penalty case, attorney argues
item.description: Attorneys for Douglas Carter, who turned 71 the same day the motion was filed, have asked a judge to dismiss the death penalty case that sent him to Utah's death row 41 years ago. The motion rests on evidence that was lost or destroyed in the 1985 killing of Eva Oleson, who was stabbed and shot in her Provo home. Judge Derek Pullan had previously vacated Carter's aggravated murder conviction after finding significant misconduct by police and prosecutors, and a day after the dismissal motion he issued a written order denying Carter bail pending a new trial. Defense attorney Neal Hamilton, who called the handling of the case by Utah County prosecutors unprecedented, also moved to compel the state to answer discovery requests dating back to fall 2025. A hearing is set for Tuesday, Sept. 22, when a trial date is expected to be finalized.
item.dc:creator: Amy Donaldson, KSL

item.title: American, United prepare further capacity trims as fuel shock reshapes flying
item.description: American Airlines and United Airlines are preparing to cut more flying if jet fuel prices stay high, as the industry absorbs a cost surge that began with the Iran war. Executives from both carriers said Wednesday that travel demand has held up even after fare increases, letting them recover much of the added fuel expense, but the latest price jump has them reevaluating less-profitable routes for late this year and possibly into 2027. American estimated the recent fuel increase alone will add roughly $1 billion to its fourth-quarter costs, while United said some December flights will be dropped with further trims possible in the first quarter. American CEO Robert Isom told a Morgan Stanley conference he felt good about the airline's forecast for third-quarter revenue growth of 16% to 19% year over year. The moves reflect a broader industry approach of protecting pricing where demand allows while removing flights whose economics deteriorate.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Kumar Singh and Shivansh Tiwary, Reuters

item.title: This year's AARP Andrus Award recipient finds purpose through music and community
item.description: Alice Cipollini, 80, of Ogden is this year's recipient of the AARP Andrus Award, which honors volunteers who have devoted themselves to strengthening their communities. Cipollini has spent the past 12 years at Give Me a Chance, an Ogden community center serving low-income families. A retired schoolteacher, she was grieving at home after her husband's death and had barely gone out for months when she answered a newspaper ad seeking an after-school tutor. She now gives private guitar and accordion lessons to students of all ages, who perform around the community at farmers markets, nursing homes, the children's museum and Bach festivals.
item.dc:creator: Tamara Vaifanua, KSL

item.title: 16 local leaders in Utah sign letter to Interior secretary, urging him to 'protect public lands'
item.description: Sixteen current and former Utah local leaders joined more than 200 officials from across the West in a letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum urging him to reverse recent public-lands policies. The letter, dated Wednesday, points to President Donald Trump's July order shrinking Utah's Grand Staircase-Escalante and Bears Ears national monuments by 90%, and raises concerns about deep agency budget and staffing cuts, a fossil-fuel-forward energy agenda, and rollbacks of the Public Lands and Roadless conservation rules. Utah signatories include Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall, Cottonwood Heights Mayor Gay Lynn Bennion, Midvale Mayor Dustin Gettel, Alta Mayor Roger Bourke and Springdale Mayor Barbara Bruno. Current and former leaders from Moab, Castle Valley, and Grand and Summit counties also signed. The signers argued the protected areas sustain local communities and underpin the region's outdoor way of life.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Man who sprayed Minnesota Rep. Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison
item.description: Anthony Kazmierczak, 56, was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison for spraying Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar with liquid at a Minneapolis town hall, matching the term prosecutors recommended under a plea deal. He also received three years of supervised release with a no-contact condition regarding Omar, and U.S. Marshals escorted him from the courtroom. Witnesses said Kazmierczak jumped up from the audience during the Jan. 27 meeting and sprayed liquid from a syringe at Omar while accusing her of splitting Minnesota apart, before her security detail tackled him and turned him over to police. Authorities determined the liquid was a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar, and he was charged with assaulting a U.S. officer; Omar was not hurt and finished the town hall. At an earlier hearing Kazmierczak told U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen his memory of the incident was fuzzy, and he later wrote to Omar apologizing for frightening her.
item.dc:creator: Tim Sullivan, Associated Press

item.title: Utah hypnotherapist, already charged with abusing patients, linked to another victim
item.description: William Del Draney, a 77-year-old West Jordan hypnotherapist already facing charges of sexually abusing patients, has been linked to an additional victim and charged with object rape, a first-degree felony, in 3rd District Court. The new charge stems from a 2010 session at Draney's residence in which prosecutors say he told a client he could see a medical condition on the man's aura, had him strip to his underwear, and framed the encounter as clinical rather than sexual before touching him inappropriately. In June, Draney was charged with nine counts of forcible sodomy and 11 counts of forcible sexual abuse; his next court date in that case is Oct. 16. Prosecutors allege he used his position of trust as a hypnotherapist to target men over nearly two decades, with reports from victims dating back to at least 2007.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: GE Aerospace confident GE9X mid-seal issue will not delay Boeing 777X entry into service
item.description: GE Aerospace Chief Financial Officer Rahul Ghai said Thursday he is confident that a durability problem with the GE9X engine's mid-seal will not delay the Boeing 777X's planned entry into service next year. GE disclosed the potential issue in February and said in April it had found the root cause and was finalizing a fix without schedule impact. Speaking at a Morgan Stanley conference, Ghai said testing showed the mid-seal, which connects the engine's front and rear sections, was less durable than expected, prompting a redesign; engines with the new seal began shipping to Boeing in the third quarter and FAA certification of the part is expected within months. He said internal testing gave the company a high degree of confidence in the redesign, which is now built into production engines. The existing seal can still be used for certification work underway, including approvals Boeing needs before starting ETOPS testing.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Biotower project proceeds on Salt Lake's west side
item.description: A biotower project on Salt Lake City's west side near 1030 W. Pierpont Ave. is moving ahead after neighborhood complaints earlier in the year prompted design changes. Salt Lake City Public Utilities deputy director Jason Brown said landscaping including trees, rocks and a 10-foot wall is already in place, with bark mulch to follow and the biotower itself scheduled for installation in January. The structure will rise about 15 feet rather than the originally planned 30, and the manufacturer agreed to produce the filter in an earth-toned tan color to help it blend into the surroundings. Utility crews say the filter is needed to treat corrosive sewer gases that also produce a rotten-egg odor. Neighbors had objected over the tower's height and appearance and its possible effects on home values and health, but Brown said no recent complaints have come in.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: NASA spacecraft discovers a huge new crater on the moon
item.description: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed a lunar crater larger than the Roman Colosseum, formed by an impact two years ago that went undetected at the time. The steep-sided hole measures about 728 feet (222 meters) across and up to 141 feet (43 meters) deep, making it the largest known impact crater created in the solar system in recent times — an event researchers estimate occurs only about once every 132 years and called effectively a once-in-a-lifetime observation in one of two studies published Wednesday in Science Advances. The orbiter photographed the crater on the moon's near side in May 2024 shortly after an asteroid or comet fragment struck, but the strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space. The wide-angle images went unnoticed in the volume of data until August 2025, with detailed follow-up imagery gathered last fall and confirmation early this year. The crater, named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston's Lunar and Planetary Institute, is three times larger than the previous record holder.
item.dc:creator: Marcia Dunn, Associated Press

item.title: Draper man says parents, sister were trying to normalize migratory status when detained by ICE
item.description: Julian Rincon, a naturalized U.S. citizen from Colombia living in Draper, is speaking out after his sister and parents were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Phoenix's Sky Harbor International Airport in late August. His sister Daniela Rincon and parents Clara Avellaneda and Henry Rincon, who live in Herriman, had work permits and were pursuing steps to normalize their immigration status when they were arrested Aug. 26 on arrival from a Salt Lake City flight for what was meant to be a short family trip. The three are being held at the Eloy Detention Center in Arizona, and the Department of Homeland Security described them in a statement as illegal aliens from Colombia. Federal records show Daniela entered the U.S. in May 2017 and her parents in August 2019, each with permission to stay for a limited period. Rincon questioned why people actively following a legal path to residency would be detained.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Ogden cold case closed after investigators obtain prison confession
item.description: Ogden police and the Weber Metro Cold Case Task Force have closed the nearly 30-year-old disappearance of Richard Roy Billmayer, who vanished in 1997 and was later listed as a missing person under suspicious circumstances in the National Crime Information Center database. Richard Annis, an inmate serving a life sentence for another homicide at Anamosa State Penitentiary in Iowa, admitted in a recorded prison confession that he killed Billmayer and disposed of his body in a dumpster. Ogden Police Detective Douglas Dunbar, a lead investigator, called the resolution surreal after a three-decade investigation. Investigator Mike Rounkles of the task force, which operates under the Weber County Attorney's Office, said the best possible outcome was the truth and the family now has it. Billmayer's niece Sabra Winters remembered him as her favorite and most fun-loving uncle.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Texas man who operated 'ghost broker' scheme sentenced to probation, deportation
item.description: Carlos David Garcia Gonzalez, 38, of Liberty Hills, Texas, was sentenced to probation and deportation for running a ghost broker insurance scheme in Utah. Charged in June in 3rd District Court with insurance fraud, communications fraud, two counts of engaging in a pattern of unlawful activity, identity fraud and forgery, he pleaded guilty Aug. 22 to insurance fraud and one pattern-of-unlawful-activity count, with the remaining four charges dismissed. In his plea statement Garcia admitted posing as a licensed agent and submitting fraudulent online data to three insurance companies to obtain auto policies out of Salt Lake County, producing roughly $832,000 in restitution from avoided premiums. Investigators say he obtained more than 1,100 auto policies and collected about $84,470 in payments for faulty or nonexistent coverage, using victims' names, birth dates and policy numbers to make unauthorized changes by phone.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah man charged with hiring hit man while awaiting trial for the same crime
item.description: Orane James Spence, 34, of Magna, already jailed on accusations that he tried to hire someone to kill his ex-wife and her mother, has been charged with attempting the same scheme from behind bars. Prosecutors filed two counts of criminal solicitation to commit murder, a first-degree felony, in 3rd District Court on Wednesday; the earlier case carrying identical charges is scheduled for trial at the end of the month. According to the new charges, Spence approached a fellow inmate at the Salt Lake County Jail on May 15 seeking someone to keep his ex-wife from testifying, saying he was desperate because he expected a lengthy prison sentence. The inmate supplied the number of a confidential informant, and Spence allegedly offered up to $50,000 and asked for a clean death that would raise no suspicion. Investigators said he tried to conceal the plot by placing calls to the informant using another inmate's calling credentials.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: UN-backed experts cite possible US war crimes in Iran strikes
item.description: A U.N.-backed fact-finding mission reported Thursday that it found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, and separately accused Iran's government of crimes against humanity against its own population. The mission, chaired by Bangladeshi jurist Sara Hossain and created in 2022 by the Geneva-based Human Rights Council, is composed of independent experts and was expected to present its findings Monday to the 47-member council. Its conclusions about U.S. conduct center on a pair of airstrikes that killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children. An Associated Press investigation found that at least one U.S. missile struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in the southern city of Minab at the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February, with Iranian state media reporting 168 killed and no final accounting yet completed. The report is not binding but adds to the international record and could support future efforts to pursue justice in international courts.
item.dc:creator: Jamey Keaten, Associated Press

item.title: Search continues for 2 missing women presumed drowned at Sand Hollow Reservoir
item.description: The search for two Las Vegas women, ages 26 and 28, presumed drowned in Sand Hollow Reservoir was set to resume at 7:30 a.m. Thursday, with a friend saying one of the women was about four and a half months pregnant with twins. The two were riding a Jet Ski Tuesday afternoon with 23-year-old Antonio Omari Lewis of Henderson, Nevada, when he crashed; none of the three wore life jackets. Lewis, a coworker of both women, was arrested and charged Wednesday in 5th District Court with two counts of automobile homicide, a second-degree felony, plus class C misdemeanors for improper navigation in a wakeless area and failing to obey waterway markers and six infractions including life-jacket, registration and invasive-mussel violations. The Utah Department of Natural Resources said the women were last seen in the southern part of the reservoir and were reported missing around 4:20 p.m. Park rangers searched roughly 90 minutes using sonar, drones and aircraft before shifting from rescue to recovery at about 5:30 p.m., and the Washington County Search and Rescue Dive Team continued without success.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah Government Records Office asks lawmakers for help to handle increasing appeals
item.description: The Utah Government Records Office told the Government Operations Interim Committee on Wednesday that public records appeals are rising fast enough that it may need more staff and more time to hold hearings and issue orders. Director Lonny Pehrson reported the office inherited 102 pending appeals when it began operating in mid-2025, a backlog built up after lawmakers abolished the State Records Committee and after that committee had gone without a quorum. In its first year the office held 170 hearings and decided 276 appeals, with another 79 withdrawn or otherwise resolved, cutting average waits for an appeal hearing from 130 days to well within the 64-day statutory guideline. But 309 new appeals were filed over the same period, which the report called a drastic increase over past years. Pehrson said filings nearly doubled starting in December, just as the office was making progress on the backlog, and have stayed well above average for six months with no sign of slowing.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Black bear euthanized in Grand Teton National Park after visitors repeatedly leave food behind
item.description: Grand Teton National Park staff euthanized a black bear near Delta Lake on Friday after visitors repeatedly let the animal obtain human food, conditioning it to approach people. Park officials said in a news release that the bear was lethally removed because of poor decisions by park visitors. Reports of the bear approaching people near Delta Lake began earlier in the year, when officials could not yet tell whether the encounters were isolated or a sign of food conditioning; the bear went on to receive human food on multiple occasions and repeatedly approached visitors. Wildlife staff stepped up monitoring and tried to haze the animal away but found it unusually hard to discourage, and managers concluded the repeated food rewards and increasingly close encounters posed an unacceptable safety risk. Because Delta Lake sits in remote backcountry, staff tranquilized and euthanized the bear on site and flew the carcass out.
item.dc:creator: EastIdahoNews.com staff

item.title: NASA says new Roman telescope's lifespan could more than double, to 22 years
item.description: NASA says the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope may be able to operate for up to 22 years, more than double the lifespan announced before its launch. The agency had previously described a five-year primary mission plus a five-year extension, supported by a 10-year fuel budget. NASA credits the longer outlook to the precision of the telescope's first mid-course correction, anticipated results from a second correction and orbital insertion still ahead, and extra fuel loaded before liftoff. Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote in an agency blog post that exquisite planning by the orbital dynamics team, execution by operations staff and a precise SpaceX launch left Roman with fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations. The observatory launched Aug. 30 from Cape Canaveral aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket and is traveling toward Lagrange Point 2 to study major questions in astrophysics and cosmology.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: Emigration Canyon residents concerned over proposed Sinclair fuel pipeline expansion
item.description: Emigration Canyon homeowners are raising concerns about HF Sinclair's proposed Westline Connect project, which could route a new refined petroleum pipeline through the area. Company representatives presented the plan to the Emigration Canyon City Council this week, and the proposal remains in early planning with no final route chosen. The project would expand the Pioneer Pipeline, which carries refined fuels into Utah from Wyoming, and the UNEV Pipeline, which moves refined products from the Salt Lake City area to Las Vegas. A company representative said the Pioneer Pipeline's existing capacity of 60,000 barrels a day would grow by another 35,000. HF Sinclair argued in a statement that fuel demand across the Mountain West has outpaced the existing pipeline network, leaving producers dependent on trucking, and that the project would steady supply and remove truck traffic from highways in four states.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: Fossil tooth analysis confirms Tyrannosaurus rex was warm-blooded
item.description: A study published Wednesday in Science Advances offers the first direct estimate of Tyrannosaurus rex's body temperature, putting it at roughly 97 degrees Fahrenheit (36 Celsius) — about the same as humans. Researchers reached the figure by analyzing chemical signatures preserved in fossilized teeth, a technique that co-author Robert Eagle, a geobiologist and associate professor at UCLA, described as the most direct constraint on T. rex body temperature achieved so far. Scientists have suspected for nearly 60 years that the predator was warm-blooded, and a T. rex footprint found in Alaska in 2022 bolstered the case by showing the animals thrived in frigid settings where cold-blooded reptiles could not. The finding supports the view that T. rex maintained an active metabolism even in cold climates. Researchers say knowing the temperature sharpens understanding of the dinosaur's behavior, physiology and interactions with other species between about 69 million and 66 million years ago.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Nicioli, CNN

item.title: Understand needs, forge solutions, President Oaks invites at Washington National Cathedral
item.description: President Dallin H. Oaks of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints spoke at the Washington National Cathedral on Wednesday, on the eve of Constitution Day, calling for common ground in preserving religious freedom. He told the audience he speaks for no political party or pressure group but for the Constitution itself, which he described as a model allowing a diverse people to govern themselves. Oaks brought seven decades of constitutional study to the address: he clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice Earl Warren, taught law for 15 years, and served more than three years on the Utah Supreme Court before his 1984 call to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He has served as an apostle for 42 years and was sustained as church president in October 2025. In his remarks he recounted early church members' expulsion from Missouri in the 1830s and their move west beyond U.S. borders in the 1840s, describing those pioneers as refugees.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Jensen, Deseret News

item.title: Salt Lake City, UDOT crafting emergency plan for flooded west side residents
item.description: Salt Lake City and the Utah Department of Transportation disagree over who is responsible for an August water main break that flooded more than a dozen Poplar Grove homes, but both are moving to help residents still displaced a month later. The Salt Lake City Council informally voted Tuesday to include a new emergency household stabilization fund of up to $50,000 in an upcoming budget amendment, authorizing staff to prepare as though the money is already allocated. Mayor Erin Mendenhall said UDOT has signaled willingness to match whatever the city contributes. The money is intended to help displaced residents secure temporary housing and cover other pressing costs. Councilman Alejandro Puy, whose district covers Poplar Grove, proposed the item and said there is an immediate need for stabilization; the discussion came a day after KSL interviewed homeowners still unable to return home.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams and Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Great Salt Lake dust expensive to manage, study finds
item.description: A University of Utah study from the Wilkes Center for Climate Science and Policy finds that dust blowing off the Great Salt Lake's exposed bed is both a growing health hazard and an expensive problem to manage. John C. Lin, the center's scientific director and an atmospheric sciences professor, said researchers used a high-resolution computer model of dust sources and wind patterns and overlaid it with population data, finding Tooele County faces the highest average exposure, followed by Salt Lake County. The study puts the collective health costs to Utahns of continued lake decline at roughly $115 million a year, with Lin noting documented cases of exposure causing missed school and work. Mitigation options the team examined ranged from engineering solutions to periodically flooding the playa and growing vegetation or installing structures to slow the wind, but costs could reach into the billions if pursued over decades. A follow-up study will examine which pollutants appear in different parts of the lakebed and at what concentrations.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Utah drivers change habits as gas prices climb
item.description: Utah drivers are paying roughly $1.50 more per gallon than a year ago, with the state average near $4.80, and new survey data suggests the prices are reshaping driving habits. LendingTree data shared with the KSL Investigators found 81% of drivers said transportation costs have changed their behavior: 31% are driving less, 38% are combining errands into fewer trips, 29% have started carpooling and 28% shop around for cheaper fuel before filling up. Drivers interviewed at Utah pumps described the prices as out of hand and brutal. The report reiterated familiar savings measures such as maintaining proper tire pressure and using gas apps to compare prices. LendingTree also suggested that drivers who have sharply cut their mileage ask their insurer whether lower annual mileage qualifies them for a reduced premium.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt and Sloan Schrage, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist hospitalized after Sandy crash
item.description: A teenage boy was critically injured Wednesday night in a collision between a motorcycle and a car in Sandy. Sandy police said the crash happened at 8 p.m. as the teen rode a motorcycle on 9000 South and collided with a car at 470 East. The motorcyclist was taken to a hospital with critical injuries. The far-right lane at 9000 South and 470 East was closed as a result. Police said the crash remains under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Dr. Nicole Saphier, Trump's 3rd surgeon general pick, grilled over vaccine stance
item.description: Dr. Nicole Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News contributor who is President Donald Trump's third nominee for surgeon general, faced sharp questioning about childhood vaccines at her Senate confirmation hearing Wednesday. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy pressed her to say whether she believed vaccines cause autism — a link scientific consensus rejects but which the administration has repeatedly sought to revisit — and Saphier replied that she does not believe childhood vaccines cause autism. Asked whether parents should give children the measles, mumps and rubella shot, she called the MMR vaccine the greatest tool for combating measles; the president recently urged spacing the shots out. Saphier described vaccines as a critical tool for preventing infection while saying she appreciated the administration's efforts to address concerns among vaccine-hesitant people. Cassidy countered that those efforts were only creating more confusion and pushed her to answer with greater clarity.
item.dc:creator: Fatima Hussein and Ali Swenson, Associated Press

item.title: Holocaust survivor shares her story of trauma, healing and faith
item.description: Sora Vigorito, the youngest known survivor of Josef Mengele's twin experiments at Auschwitz, spoke at the University of Utah to one of the largest audiences she has ever addressed. Rabbi Moshe Nigri, who first reached out to her, said roughly 1,500 people had signed up before reservations closed for lack of space; about 900 attended in person in the Student Union building and another 200 to 300 joined remotely. The program opened with prelude music from a quartet of LDS Institute of Religion musicians, followed by remarks from Nigri, his wife, University Interfaith Initiatives executive director Charlie Freedman, and Ethan Smith, president of Chabad on Campus at the university. Vigorito, who was nearly killed before she turned four, told the audience she has no memory of her mother, who disappeared with her older sister while begging for food and was likely seized by the Nazis. She survived in hiding with her grandmother.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Park City synagogue vandalized; hate-crime enhancement considered
item.description: Temple Har Shalom in Park City is rebuilding its sign after vandals damaged it over Labor Day weekend, days before the Jewish community observed Rosh Hashanah. Letters were torn off and the Star of David was damaged. Rabbi Jeff Dreifus said the attack was surprising given how long Jews have been part of the fabric of life in Park City, and that it left congregants feeling deliberately targeted and unsafe practicing Judaism in what they consider their Jewish home in the mountains. The Summit County Sheriff's Office is investigating the case as criminal mischief, which covers intentional damage to another person's property, and is weighing whether a victim-targeting or hate-crime enhancement applies; the Summit County Attorney's Office would make the final charging decision. Dreifus said it is the first public display of antisemitism against the congregation he can recall.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Whole grains are good for your heart. How do you know if you're eating enough?
item.description: A new analysis published Tuesday in the European Heart Journal reviewed dozens of studies to determine how whole grains benefit cardiovascular and metabolic health and how much people need to eat. The researchers found benefits begin at about 90 grams, or three servings, per day — roughly two slices of whole wheat bread plus a bowl of oatmeal — with four to six servings producing stronger effects. People who ate three to six servings daily for periods ranging from two weeks to two years showed slight improvements in about a dozen health markers, including total and LDL cholesterol, blood pressure, body weight and waist circumference, all tied to cardiovascular risk. Researcher Dagfinn Aune said that although the individual effects were small, together they corroborate what large population studies have shown. Two decades of research have already linked whole-grain-rich diets to lower risks of heart disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Schupak, CNN

item.title: Intermountain Health to convert West Valley City building into new medical campus
item.description: Intermountain Health announced Tuesday that it has acquired the nine-story Fairbourne building, one of West Valley City's largest complexes, and will convert it into a medical campus and healthcare hub in the city's downtown. To be called the Intermountain Health Fairbourne Campus, the facility will offer primary care along with oncology, orthopedics, neurology, cardiology, gastroenterology and rheumatology services. Interior construction is already underway, with multiple clinics and services expected to open later this year and a freestanding emergency department affiliated with LDS Hospital slated for late 2027. Eric Liston, president of Intermountain Health's canyons region, said the investment reflects a commitment to meet people where they are and bring more services closer to home as needs in West Valley City and western Salt Lake County evolve. LDS Hospital President Heather Wall said growing communities in western Utah need convenient access to care.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah dad turns daughter's Type 1 diabetes experience into push for a cure
item.description: Devin Holt of Salem, Utah County, is channeling his daughter's Type 1 diabetes into advocacy for a cure after a diagnosis that nearly cost her life. His daughter Caroline, now 7, was about 10 months old when he woke to find her struggling to breathe; she was in diabetic ketoacidosis with blood sugar above 600, and the family's pediatric endocrinologist told them she had roughly six hours left. With no family history of the disease, the Holts had to teach themselves how to manage a condition Devin described as a terrifying and overwhelming upending of life as they knew it. Type 1 diabetes is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin, and the CDC estimates about 2.1 million Americans have been diagnosed with it. Caroline now manages her blood sugar with an insulin pump and glucose monitor and stays active with basketball, tennis, biking and scootering.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Smithfield Utah Temple will open to the public next spring ahead of dedication
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Monday that the Smithfield Utah Temple will be dedicated April 18, 2027, by Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, after nearly five years of construction. A public open house will run Feb. 25 through March 27, preceded by a media day Feb. 22 and invited-guest tours Feb. 23 and 24. The three-story, 81,000-square-foot building sits at 800 West and 100 North and will be the second temple in Cache County, which has not received a new one since the Logan Utah Temple was completed in 1884. Then-President Russell M. Nelson announced the temple in April 2021, and ground was broken in June 2022 at a ceremony attended by Elder Cook and Elder Gary E. Stevenson. Utah now has 32 temples in operation, under construction or renovation, or announced.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah Catholic Conference to gather Catholics from across Utah
item.description: The Catholic Diocese of Salt Lake City will hold its third annual Utah Catholic Conference on Saturday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the Skaggs Catholic Center in Draper, drawing Catholics from across the state. Bishop Oscar A. Solis will preside, describing the gathering as a chance for the diocese to come together as one church to learn, pray and strengthen their faith. This year's theme is 'Sacred Heart, Heart of the Mission,' and Crystal Painter, director of the diocese's Marriage and Family Life Office, said attendees look forward to convening from throughout Utah. The event began as a training session restricted to diocesan leaders before the bishop opened it to the public three years ago, and Painter said it has grown each year as part of Solis's emphasis on comprehensive faith formation at every stage of life. Attendees can park at Juan Diego Catholic High School and travel to the nearby Skaggs center for a morning Mass with the bishop.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Impaired driver accused of driving wrong-way on 2 Salt Lake streets
item.description: An Eagle Mountain man, Sione Popi Aholelei, 23, was arrested early Sunday in Salt Lake City after allegedly driving the wrong way on two downtown streets and nearly striking a police officer. A Utah Highway Patrol trooper spotted Aholelei's vehicle speeding the wrong way on 500 South before it turned onto 600 South and skidded to a stop on a sidewalk. Police said Aholelei smelled of alcohol, had slurred speech and admitted to driving the wrong way after drinking at a nightclub; a breath test measured his blood-alcohol level at 0.190%, nearly four times the legal limit. He was booked into the Salt Lake County Jail on suspicion of DUI, driving the wrong way and being an alcohol-restricted driver, and court records show he pleaded guilty to a prior impaired-driving charge in Utah County about a year earlier.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah students to have a say in AI school policies around the state
item.description: Utah high schoolers in grades 10 through 12 are being invited to help shape how artificial intelligence is used in their schools through a new essay contest. The Sutherland Institute, led by president and CEO Todd Weiler, is running the competition, offering cash prizes of $1,000, $500 and $250 for the top three entries. Twenty-nine student delegates, one for each state Senate district, will also be chosen to debate AI policy proposals at a Utah Student AI Policy Congress at the Capitol on Nov. 20 and 21, with a resulting resolution presented to lawmakers and school boards. Applications are due Oct. 1, and winners and delegates will be announced Oct. 15.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: 2 arrested, including wanted fugitive, and accused of fighting with police
item.description: Taylorsville police arrested a wanted parole fugitive and a woman traveling with him early Monday after a violent struggle during a traffic stop near 4500 South Redwood Road. Officers say passenger Marco Dunigan, who had an active felony Board of Pardons warrant, ran from the car and fought two officers, at one point reaching for an officer's gun before he was subdued with a Taser and handcuffed. Driver Jaycie Nichole Reed, 33, was booked into the Salt Lake County Jail on suspicion of obstruction of justice after police say she got out of the vehicle, refused commands and interfered with the arrest even after being threatened with a Taser.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Driver with denied license arrested in fatal hit-and-run crash
item.description: A 53-year-old South Salt Lake man, James Shama Pulale, was arrested early Saturday in connection with a fatal hit-and-run that killed a pedestrian near 3265 South 900 West the night before. Investigators matched a broken side mirror found at the scene to a Toyota Sienna and used nearby surveillance video showing a van circling the area to trace the vehicle to a carport at Pulale's home, where they found matching damage. Police say Pulale, whose driver's license was denied for a medical condition, admitted to hitting the man, not stopping to help, and wiping evidence off the vehicle's hood. He was booked into the Salt Lake County Jail on charges including leaving the scene of an accident involving death, obstruction of justice and driving on a denied license.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Pentagon: Male, female troops must pass identical fitness tests to serve in 'combat arms' jobs
item.description: The Pentagon has formally adopted "sex-neutral" physical fitness standards for troops assigned to front-line "combat arms" jobs such as infantry soldiers, Navy SEALs, Marine riflemen and Air Force combat rescue officers. The policy, championed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, replaces the Department of Defense's 2022 fitness program and requires all active-duty service members to undergo fitness evaluations twice a year. Troops in combat arms roles must now score an average of 70% across all elements of their service-specific fitness test regardless of gender, while fitness minimums for noncombat personnel will still be adjusted by sex and age. The change follows years of debate dating back to a 2015 Pentagon decision opening all combat jobs to women.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: 'You have time': Cedar City custom butcher advocates for respectful hunting, harvesting practices
item.description: Shawn Slaugh, owner of Mountain Man Meats, a custom butcher shop in Cedar City, is urging hunters to slow down and properly care for game animals after the harvest rather than rushing the process. Slaugh, who has processed close to 1,000 wild game animals a year since opening his shop in 2022, said many hunters focus on hunter-safety certification but get little training on field-dressing and meat care, leading to spoiled meat from delays, improper cooling or dragging carcasses behind vehicles. He advises hunters to process animals quickly, avoid spraying meat with water before cutting, and take care while skinning to avoid contamination, adding that treating a harvested animal with respect is part of ethical hunting. Slaugh, also a member of the historical reenactment group American Mountain Men, said better education on post-harvest care could improve hunting's public reputation.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: UHP offers safety reminders following 2 fatal motorcycle crashes
item.description: Two motorcyclists died in separate Utah crashes on the same Saturday, prompting the Utah Highway Patrol to renew safety warnings for riders. A 52-year-old man died after a crash during the annual Fire Ride, a firefighter memorial ride that draws 300 to 400 participants between Sandy and Ogden; he was not wearing a helmet. Hours later, a 56-year-old Colorado man died on I-15 north of Beaver after failing to negotiate a curve and striking a traffic sign, though he was wearing a helmet and wind may have contributed to the crash. UHP Sgt. McCall Christensen urged motorcyclists to wear safety gear, obey speed limits, avoid distractions and maintain safe following distances, noting investigators are still probing both crashes.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: The size of 20 Costcos: Can Utah residents drive a data center out of their backyard?
item.description: Residents of the small town of Mona in Juab County say they were blindsided by a massive data center project, dubbed "Nebo North LLC" and costing at least $10 billion, that was approved for land just outside town with almost no public notice. County officials approved the project via a conditional use permit at an April hearing that lasted only four minutes with no member of the public in attendance, unlike the more heavily regulated zoning-change process that requires mailed notices to nearby landowners. Resident Taylor Flake said he only learned of the data center's scale after a gas company representative asked to run a pipeline across his property to supply a new power plant built to serve it. Neighbor Tiffanie McAfee found that conditional use permits, which carry lighter notification requirements than standard zoning changes, have been used almost exclusively in the Mona area, fueling residents' frustration that they were denied the kind of input given to other Utah communities facing similar projects, such as Dog Valley near Nephi.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: How Salt Lake travelers feel about TSA's new Gateside program
item.description: The Transportation Security Administration's new Gateside program, which lets unticketed TSA PreCheck members pass through security to greet or send off travelers at the gate, has come to Salt Lake City International Airport as one of 13 participating airports nationwide. The free program marks one of the first rollbacks of restricted post-security access for non-passengers since security tightened after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, though it requires PreCheck membership, which costs $60 to $80 for five years. Travelers interviewed at the Salt Lake airport had mixed reactions: some, like Kristi Johnson, said they wished the option had existed when their children returned from missions for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, but worried it could make gate areas more crowded. Others, such as traveler Davie Merkeley, welcomed the change, saying it could save people the hassle of buying and refunding tickets just to reach the gate.
item.dc:creator: Emily Walker, Deseret News

item.title: Utah business leader shares firsthand 9/11 account 25 years later
item.description: A Utah business leader named Crittenden is publicly sharing his account of surviving the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks for the first time in 25 years. Crittenden was working on the 51st floor of the American Express building near the World Trade Center when he watched a hijacked plane strike the North Tower at 8:46 a.m., and said American Express CEO Kenneth Chenault's decision to quickly evacuate the building's roughly 5,000 employees likely saved many lives. Crittenden was among the last four coworkers still in the building, on the 47th floor, when the South Tower collapsed, and he recalled the panic of feeling the building sway and witnessing people fleeing the devastation. He said the memory of first responders running toward danger, and the resilience of those who later returned to rebuild in Lower Manhattan, has stayed with him for a quarter century.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: What is the American sound? How the Moab Music Festival explores identity through nature
item.description: The Moab Music Festival's 2026 season, themed "This Land" in honor of the 250th anniversary of American independence, explores American musical identity through concerts staged in dramatic natural settings, including a grotto in Canyonlands National Park reachable only by riverboat. At a "Grotto I: Fantasy" performance on Sept. 3, musicians including violinists Tessa Lark and Geneva Lewis, pianists Inon Barnatan and Peter Dugan, and cellist Jay Campbell played pieces spanning the 1700s to the 2010s inside the acoustically vivid rock formation. Festival artistic director Lark and violinist Lewis said the American sound is defined less by a single style than by the diversity of the country's people and its landscapes. The festival's crew adheres to a strict leave-no-trace ethic, hauling equipment in and out by boat and sweeping away footprints so the site remains untouched between performances.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer, Deseret News

item.title: This St. George business owner is offering VHS rentals for nostalgic experience
item.description: McKay Murdock, owner of Legacy Media Digital in St. George, is renting out VHS tapes and VCRs to give families a nostalgic, screen-free movie night experience reminiscent of trips to Blockbuster. Murdock, whose business has focused since 2009 on digitizing old family photos and videos, said he wanted to counter a household where everyone is "on different screens" by encouraging families to pick a movie together and watch it without distractions. He has about 500 VHS tapes available to rent, with thousands more in storage, and said the rental program also helps keep old tapes out of landfills since many secondhand stores won't accept them. His daughter, Haylee Murdock, who works at the store despite not growing up in the VHS era, said the tactile experience of choosing and playing a tape has been a fun bonding activity for customers.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: US teen reading scores fall to lowest level in nearly 25 years
item.description: U.S. teenagers' reading scores have fallen to their lowest level in nearly 25 years, according to a new international study from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development that tested about 760,000 15-year-olds across 91 countries. American reading scores dropped 14 points since 2022, equivalent to roughly half a year of schooling, while global reading, math and science scores have all declined since 2012. At Bear Lake High School in Montpelier, Idaho, teacher Emi Wilkes and students said constant smartphone use has shortened attention spans and made sustained reading harder, though Wilkes said a broader lack of enthusiasm for reading, not just technology, is also to blame. Students also pointed to unengaging assigned reading material as another reason many teens have soured on books.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: In an age of instant answers, educators say there's a case for letting kids struggle a little
item.description: Developmental experts and educators argue that children need room to wrestle with everyday problems — a forgotten lunch, a hard math problem, an unfamiliar route — because problem-solving is a skill built through practice. The difficulty for parents is distinguishing between helping a child through a hard situation and eliminating the problem before the child gets a chance to try. That line has grown harder to hold now that an answer or AI-generated help is available within seconds. Technology has also given parents more ways to monitor their children, including location tracking, real-time grade access and instant email to teachers, which can prompt intervention before a child even notices something is wrong. Experts say what independence looks like varies with a child's age, abilities and circumstances, but generally means learning to plan, make decisions, solve problems, recover from mistakes and decide what to do next.
item.dc:creator: Cheyanne Mumphrey, Associated Press

item.title: Utah Youth Sports Giving Day launches during Salt Lake Bees Game
item.description: Utah Youth Sports Giving Day launched Saturday night during a Salt Lake Bees game at America First Square in South Jordan, bringing together about 160 youth sports organizations. The campaign's initial $1 million public fundraising goal was met within 10 minutes of the public launch, part of a larger $3 million effort led by Miller Sports + Entertainment, the Larry H. & Gail Miller Family Foundation and the Daniels Fund, with at least $1.5 million in matching funds pledged by partners including Utah 2034. Organizers such as Utah Crew's Victoria Rojo and Adaptive Arena's Ashley Guymon said the funds will help offset costs like registration fees, equipment and specialized gear that can otherwise keep children, including those with special needs, from playing sports. Miller Sports + Entertainment president Michelle Smith and Utah 2034 Olympics and Paralympics Organizing Committee's Abby Osborne said the effort reflects a broader commitment to expanding kids' access to sports across the state.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Brigham City Peach Days continues despite local peach crop loss
item.description: Brigham City's 122-year-old Peach Days festival went on this year despite a spring freeze that wiped out the local peach crop, forcing organizers to source peaches from Idaho growers instead. Box Elder Chamber of Commerce aide Katia Holdway said the event still drew roughly 70,000 visitors for its parade, classic car show, vendors and entertainment. Peach Days CEO Cari Tagge called the crop loss heartbreaking but said neighboring Idaho farmers stepped in to keep the festival's peach-themed offerings intact. Organizers say attendance and vendor sales held steady, and they're hopeful next year's harvest will restore the tradition's homegrown peaches.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: First Presbyterian Church of Salt Lake City teaches about legacy amid ongoing growth
item.description: The First Presbyterian Church of Salt Lake City, whose congregation dates to an 1871 Presbyterian mission founded by Reverend Josiah Welch, is experiencing renewed growth even as it marks more than 120 years in its red-sandstone building on C Street and South Temple. Senior Pastor Jamie White, the congregation's first female senior pastor, and Pastoral Associate Jared McClure detailed the building's 1902-1906 construction, its Red Butte Canyon sandstone, and Scottish Presbyterian traditions like the annual Kirkin' o' th' Tartan, which draws about 1,500 worshippers each October. Facilities manager Jim Sweeney described ongoing preservation work, including stained-glass and pipe-organ repairs estimated at around $5 million. Church leaders said the building's blend of century-old heritage and current growth reflects both its history and an open, welcoming culture drawing new members.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Why Salt Lake City is seeking to sell over 950 acres near its airport to the state
item.description: Salt Lake City is pursuing a plan to sell more than 950 acres of city-owned land near Salt Lake City International Airport to the Utah Department of Natural Resources, with a conservation easement to protect Great Salt Lake wetlands from future development. Airport senior planning director Brady Fredrickson told the City Council the land, acquired in 1995 with FAA grant funding, is valued between $3.8 million and $5.1 million, and airport director Bill Wyatt said the nonprofit Utah Open Lands would hold the easement. City officials, including Mayor Erin Mendenhall's office, back the deal as a way to preserve wetlands buffers around the lake, and proceeds would help fund a planned runway extension. A council public hearing is tentatively set for Oct. 6, with a vote possible by Oct. 20 and a sale as early as November, pending FAA and Army Corps of Engineers approval.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Why are Americans giving the nation's K-12 schools a 'Needs Improvement' grade?
item.description: A new Gallup poll found only 32% of Americans are satisfied with the quality of K-12 education nationally, the lowest mark in the poll's 27-year history and part of a broader decline that researchers like Michigan State's Sarah Reckhow and UMass Amherst's Jack Schneider tied to falling test scores, AI anxieties and fights over Trump administration education policy. The Trump administration, including Education Secretary Linda McMahon, countered that its school choice expansions and new education freedom tax credit are restoring confidence after what it called poor outcomes under the Biden administration. Gallup's Zach Hrynowski said the findings reflect broader institutional distrust rather than education specifically, and the poll showed sharp satisfaction gaps by income, education level, party and race, with Democrats driving most of the recent decline. Parents of current K-12 students remained comparatively more satisfied at 66%, though even that figure fell nearly 10 points from last year. Utah State Superintendent Molly Hart said the results underscore that public trust in education must be continually earned.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: 'We woke up to total devastation': Utah family details Kauai hurricane experience
item.description: A St. George family of 17 vacationing on Kauai's north shore rode out Hurricane Lowell in an Airbnb, describing cracking trees and fears the doors would blow open before waking to widespread destruction, downed power lines and days without electricity. Family members Angaleza Adams and Rocky Bunker said they helped neighbors repair storm-damaged roofs and later faced a chaotic departure, including a canceled flight and an overnight stay at the airport after TSA screening was hampered by a single generator and repeated power outages. Despite the disruption, the family said they were struck by acts of kindness among stranded travelers and local residents helping each other recover. The Hawaii State Tourism Authority has urged visitors to postpone trips to Kauai or consider other islands while cleanup continues.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist dies in crash during motorcade honoring fallen firefighters
item.description: A 52-year-old Tooele County man died Saturday after a motorcycle crash on Highway 89 near Layton's Gordon Avenue exit during the 2026 Fire Ride, an annual motorcade of 300 to 400 riders honoring fallen firefighters that traveled from Sandy through Davis County to Ogden's Fallen Firefighter Memorial. The Utah Department of Public Safety said the man, who was not wearing a helmet, died en route to the hospital in a chain-reaction crash that also involved two other motorcyclists whose injuries were not immediately known. KSL noted the story would be updated as more details emerge.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: 9-month-pregnant Utah mom aims to run mile in under 5 minutes
item.description: Highland runner Makenna Myler, a former BYU standout and professional Asics athlete, is training to run a sub-5-minute mile on Oct. 7 while nine months pregnant with her third child, aiming to beat her own women's world-best mark of 5:17 set during her second pregnancy. The event, called Sub 5 at 9 at Provo High School, invites others to "race a pregnant woman" to raise money for For All Mothers, a nonprofit supporting mothers in sports through lactation stations and childcare grants. Myler, who trains under longtime BYU coach Ed Eyestone and has personal bests of 4:37 in the mile and 2:26:14 in the marathon, said the effort is less about records than showing what women can accomplish with support. She said her pregnancy is healthy and that she has learned to balance training intensity and recovery differently than in her earlier pregnancies.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: St. George hospital expands services for cancer, seeks to reduce helicopter response times
item.description: Intermountain Health celebrated two expansions at St. George Regional Hospital this week: a new emergency flight-and-ambulance base meant to cut helicopter response times by five to 10 minutes, and an enlarged cancer center adding neuro-oncology care, dedicated infusion space and expanded supportive services. Dr. Terence Rhodes, the region's senior oncology medical director, said the cancer center growth reflects a commitment to treating "the whole person," including new neuro-oncology care from Dr. Colby Cevering. Flight and ambulance operations manager Rex Jacobsen said consolidating previously scattered crews, equipment and supplies into one facility near the ER will let responders reach patients faster across a 150-mile radius around St. George. Both projects marked ribbon cuttings this week as part of Intermountain's broader investment in southern Utah's growing healthcare needs.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Trump reduced Bears Ears by 91%. What does the law really say?
