item.description: Conservation and outdoor-recreation groups, including Patagonia and the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, moved on Sept. 2 to reactivate a 2017 lawsuit after President Trump's Proclamation 11043 cut Bears Ears National Monument by 91% from its 1.3 million acres, arguing the 1906 Antiquities Act gives presidents power only to create monuments, not shrink them. Utah Department of Natural Resources deputy commissioner Redge Johnson defended the reduction, arguing sprawling monuments like Bears Ears lack adequate funding and management compared with smaller sites like Natural Bridges. Attorneys Steve Bloch and Aaron Weiss countered that Congress reserved the power to alter monument boundaries for itself, and critics said the rollback mainly benefits mining interests amid new mining-claim filings. A Deseret News/Hinckley Institute poll found 56% of Utah voters opposed shrinking the monument, though most also said they prefer state or local control of public lands over federal management.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Park City School District IT employee arrested for child sex abuse material
item.description: Garrett Blaine Harmon, 29, an IT systems administrator for the Park City School District, was booked into the Utah County Jail on 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor after a UK child-exploitation investigation traced encrypted chats to him via facial recognition on a photo he shared. According to a police booking affidavit, Harmon admitted in the messages to a sexual interest in children and to previously abusing several boys during a group camping trip, and investigators say he distributed roughly five self-depicting images and 18 files of apparent child sexual abuse material to a UK suspect. Homeland Security agents found Harmon's Eagle Mountain home vacant and for sale before locating him in Heber City, and the affidavit notes he had direct access to children through his school district IT role.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Tooele life coach who admitted to sexually abusing clients gets consecutive prison sentences
item.description: Douglas Richens, 53, a former life coach and co-owner of the Tooele wellness business Gray Space Experts, was sentenced Aug. 10 to 10 consecutive one-to-15-year prison terms after pleading guilty to sexually abusing six girls, guaranteeing at least a decade behind bars. Third District Judge Douglas Hogan's consecutive sentence followed a February plea deal in which Richens admitted to touching the girls' genital areas, dropping two more serious first-degree felony charges; charging documents describe a pattern investigators said resembled grooming, uncovered after a client reported inappropriate touching during a session. The investigation expanded to include a teen client and a decade-old complaint from 2020 that a family had initially asked to close before deciding to press charges. Richens, who held no medical or counseling license, was also ordered to have no contact with his victims.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah family that lost loved ones on 9/11 tell their story to keep history alive
item.description: Margaret Wahlstrom and her daughter Mallory Wahlstrom Wright of Kaysville continue sharing the story of losing family members Mary Alice Wahlstrom and Carolyn Beug, who died when their hijacked flight struck the World Trade Center's north tower on 9/11. Wright, who was a seventh-grader at the time, recalls looking up to her aunt Beug, a Disney Studios employee. The two women say they've spent 25 years retelling the story, including at local schools, because they fear the unity and compassion the country felt after the attacks have faded amid today's social-media-driven division. Wahlstrom keeps a piece of recovered World Trade Center steel as a symbol of resilience that she says is stronger than any structure.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: U. grad with stage 4 cancer heads to Washington to push for clinical trial access
item.description: North Salt Lake resident Joseph Mutalwa, a University of Utah graduate originally from Uganda, was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer in 2025 during his final year of school after months of worsening pain and other symptoms. Despite the diagnosis and a lengthy hospital stay, he completed his bachelor's degree and is now pursuing a master's at Boston University while participating in a clinical trial in Salt Lake City. After meeting Utah Gov. Spencer Cox in May, Mutalwa is traveling to Washington, D.C. this month with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network to lobby Utah's congressional delegation for more cancer research funding and passage of the Clinical Trial Modernization Act, which would ease financial and geographic barriers to trial access.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: United or divided? Speakers urge unity at Utah 9/11 memorial ceremony
item.description: Utahns gathered at the state Capitol Friday for a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, where Gov. Spencer Cox questioned whether the country would respond to a similar tragedy today with the same unity it showed in 2001 rather than immediate partisan blame. Norm Wahlstrom, who lost his mother and sister aboard the hijacked flight that hit the World Trade Center's north tower, told the crowd that the outpouring of kindness after the attacks felt like a truly united America, drawing a standing ovation. Retired Utah National Guard Maj. Gen. Brian Tarbet, who was in Washington, D.C. that day, warned that the “never forget” message has faded and said the country remains in a long struggle to defend freedom. The Utah National Guard's 23rd Army Band and a bagpiper performed at the ceremony.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: University of Utah extends accord with Ute tribe to use Utes name for sports teams
item.description: The University of Utah has extended its formal agreement with the Ute Indian Tribe governing use of the Utes name for its athletic teams for another five years, through 2031, building on an accord dating to 2003 and the tribe's support for the name since 1972. Under the new memorandum, the university will continue paying the tribe $100,000 annually, more than double scholarship funding for eligible Ute students to $18,000 a year, and extend eligibility beyond strict tribal membership to include descendants. Fourteen students qualified for the scholarship this year, up from three last year, and the university also pledged to send mobile health clinics to the Uintah and Ouray reservation up to three times annually. University athletics director Mark Harlan and other officials framed the deal as an example of a state university partnering respectfully with a sovereign nation.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Utah 9/11 first responders share memories at South Jordan remembrance project
item.description: A 9/11 remembrance exhibit in South Jordan is giving Utahns who responded to Ground Zero 25 years ago a place to share their memories with younger generations. Former New York Fire Department Lt. Steven Casquarelli and former NYPD Sgt. Scott Zink both described rushing toward the World Trade Center after the attacks and spending days searching the rubble, recalling the eerie silence broken only by the alarms of motionless firefighters' equipment. Zink said he and other responders knew immediately from the scale of the damage that an airliner, not a small plane, had hit the towers. The free exhibit runs through Monday.

item.title: How Utah's first Olympics helped the world heal after 9/11
item.description: As the nation marked 25 years since 9/11, this look back revisits the moment a tattered flag recovered from the World Trade Center was carried into a silent Rice-Eccles Stadium at the opening of the 2002 Salt Lake Winter Olympics while the Tabernacle Choir performed the national anthem. Olympic speedskater Derek Parra, one of the flag bearers, and 2002 organizing committee figures like Fraser Bullock recalled the moment as deeply emotional and unifying for the world just months after the attacks. Retired speedskater Julie Letai, now on the 2034 Salt Lake organizing committee but too young to remember 9/11 firsthand, said hearing Parra's account gave her new appreciation for what the Games meant. The inclusion of the flag was contentious behind the scenes — the IOC rejected carrying it during the parade of nations — but organizers say the lesson of using the Olympics as a unifying force will guide Utah's 2034 Games.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Roy crossing guard faces long recovery after being hit by car
item.description: Roy crossing guard Kate McLean remains hospitalized with broken bones in both legs and her right shoulder after being struck by a car and slammed into a power pole near Freedom Elementary on Sept. 4, an incident her fellow crossing guard and friend Lilly Shearer witnessed. McLean, a mother of six including a 1-year-old, is expected to be out of work for months, and Shearer has started an online fundraiser to help cover household costs beyond what workers' compensation pays. Shearer said the intersection lacks a dedicated turn signal and isn't marked as a school zone despite heavy foot traffic, and she's urging drivers to slow down near crossing guards regardless. KSL has asked Roy police for updates on the driver involved.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: 25 years after 9/11, Utah firefighters who responded remember the call
item.description: Six Utah firefighters who deployed to Ground Zero with Utah Task Force 1 after the Sept. 11 attacks — now serving as chiefs and captains with the Salt Lake City Fire Department and Unified Fire Authority — reflected on the 25th anniversary of the attacks. Division Chief Bob Silverthorne and colleagues recalled where they were when the towers were hit, the realization they were being deployed, and the sobering awareness that 343 fellow firefighters had died in New York. The team spent 10 days working at Ground Zero, where they said they had to earn the trust of New York's fire department before being given more responsibility, marking their helmets with Maltese crosses to signal they too were firefighters. They also remembered the outpouring of public support they received on the streets of New York during their deployment.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: 16-year-old girl flies American flag on horseback honor 9/11
item.description: For the sixth year in a row, 16-year-old Cherade Allred of Lake Point in Tooele County rode her horse through the community Friday carrying an American flag to honor victims of the Sept. 11 attacks. Her mother, Chaelea Allred, recalled watching the second plane hit the World Trade Center from her school classroom and said a relative was near the south tower when it was struck; the family also has generations of military service. Chaelea said donations have helped the family buy more flags for the annual ride, and she hopes to eventually display 2,977 of them — one for every victim. Cherade planned to ride again Saturday into a nearby memorial breakfast.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: 'Maintaining traditions': Utah State Fair celebrates 170 years
item.description: The Utah State Fair is marking its 170th year, with longtime butter sculptor Matt McNaughtan unveiling his 19th butter cow — this year depicting a cow bursting from a birthday cake — using roughly 600 pounds of butter that gets frozen and reused annually. Fair deputy executive director Nicki Claeys said preserving traditions, from agricultural contests to fiber arts demonstrations, is central to the fair's identity even as some specific activities have evolved over the decades. Claeys said she treasures artifacts fairgoers bring in, like poultry ribbons from the 1930s a family recently discovered, and this year's 170th-anniversary celebration includes surprise prize giveaways and throwback entertainment such as an extreme lumberjack show.
